Israeli forces hold about 65 Lebanese towns and villages in the south (The National, 8 October 2026). Estimates differ: about 570-600 sq km by the Reuters-based figure used on Wikipedia, 'roughly one-fifth of Lebanon' per Al Jazeera on 27 June; evacuation orders cover about 2,000 sq km. Netanyahu (15 June): they stay 'for as long as necessary'. More than 1.2 million Lebanese are displaced.

Israeli forces hold a security zone in southern Syria - nine bases and outposts from Mount Hermon to Daraa and Quneitra (ACLED, June 2026), 84 ground incursions in May 2026 alone - and Defence Minister Katz said in June 2026 that the troops stay for an unlimited period.

Israel holds about 60% of the Gaza Strip behind a Yellow Line that has been pushed toward the coast, against the 50% the plan allowed and about 53% in the first days of the ceasefire; Defence Minister Katz said in Dec 2025 that the army 'will never fully leave'. The figure is the share of the Strip under Israeli control, not a deployment size.

levers.summary: Emirati ground forces in Yemen: none since January 2026 (the UAE says its mission ended), after more than a decade; the status of the UAE-linked airbase on Mayyun/Perim reported in 2021 is unclear.

The UN group of experts' 2024 report put 3,000-4,000 Rwanda Defence Force troops in eastern DRC operating alongside M23; the July 2025 report gave no new figure and found 'de facto direction and effective control'. Rwanda denies the deployment while calling its presence 'defensive measures'; no 2026 figure was found.

China's holdings of US Treasury securities fell to USD 633.4bn in June 2026 (from USD 731.4bn a year earlier, -13.4%), the third largest foreign holder after Japan and the United Kingdom and the lowest level in the current TIC table.
Iraq made its final war-reparation payment to Kuwait on 13 Jan 2022, ending a UN Compensation Commission claim of USD 52.4bn arising from the 1990 invasion; the UN declared Iraq to have fully paid.

Gazprom claims Moldovagaz owes USD 709m (USD 433m principal and USD 276m penalties, accumulated since the 1990s); a Sept 2023 audit commissioned by Chișinău puts it at USD 8.6m. Gazprom holds 50% plus one share of Moldovagaz, Transnistria 13%.

Russia still supplied 12.5% of EU gas imports in 2025 (36 bcm; about 40% by pipeline in 2021) and the Regulation of 26 Jan 2026 ends it - long-term LNG from 1 Jan 2027, pipeline gas by 30 Sep 2027; Hungary and Slovakia have sued. Oil is under a price cap lowered to USD 44.10 from 1 Feb 2026 and 632 shadow-fleet tankers are listed.

Russia still supplied 12.5% (36.0 bcm) of EU gas imports in 2025 (pipeline about 6%, LNG 13.5% of LNG imports) against about 40% by pipeline in 2021; the Regulation of 26 Jan 2026 ends it: short-term contracts from 25 Apr/17 Jun 2026, long-term LNG from 1 Jan 2027, pipeline gas by 30 Sep 2027.

Russian pipeline gas to Austria has been zero since 1 Jan 2025, after Gazprom stopped OMV (16 Nov 2024) and Ukraine did not renew transit; imports now come mainly via Germany (Norwegian pipeline gas and LNG) and Italy. E-Control rated winter 2025/26 secure; storage held 44 TWh on 24 Mar 2025 and 82.8 TWh had been injected by 8 Sep 2025.

Zeebrugge's terminal with dedicated Yamal LNG storage was the top EU importer of Russian LNG cargoes in the first half of 2026; CREA reports that Belgium cut its Russian LNG imports to zero in August 2026, ahead of the EU ban on long-term contracts from 1 Jan 2027. The two reports are not fully consistent (no official Belgian figure found).

Czech crude imports from Russia are now zero. The Druzhba pipeline had supplied about half of imports until spring 2025; it stopped in March 2025 (payment problems after US sanctions, state reserves of 330,000 t released to Orlen Unipetrol) and Czechia declared itself independent of Russian oil in April 2025, after the TAL pipeline upgrade raised capacity to 8 Mt a year.

Direct imports of Russian gas were declared zero from 2023 (replaced by Norwegian gas and Dutch and Belgian LNG); Bloomberg found in Nov 2024 that some Russian molecules still reached Czechia indirectly via Slovakia, so the zero is a statement about contracts, not about every molecule.

Russian natural gas stopped on 21 May 2022 when Gasum refused to pay in roubles; before the cutoff Russia covered about 70% of Gasum's requirements. Finland replaced it with the Balticconnector and a floating LNG terminal at Inkoo (operating since 2023), which proved its worth when the Balticconnector was cut in October 2023.

Russian electricity, about a tenth of Finnish consumption, was cut to zero in May 2022 (Fingrid curbed capacity from 1.3 GW to 900 MW in April; the supplier RAO Nordic stopped on 14 May). Olkiluoto 3 (1.6 GW, test production March 2022) replaced a large share of the imports.

Sakhalin-2 LNG supplies about 9% of Japan's LNG imports under contracts running to 2028-2033; Mitsui (12.5%) and Mitsubishi (10%) hold stakes that Tokyo has kept, arguing a break would hand them to Chinese firms; Sakhalin Blend crude is exempt from the G7 price cap for Japan.

Russian natural gas has been banned in Latvia since 1 Jan 2023; the Baltic-Finnish gas market now runs almost entirely on LNG through Klaipeda, Inkoo and Hamina, the last Russian LNG cargo arrived in July 2024, and Russian gas survives only as transit to Kaliningrad through Lithuania.
Russia's share of Dutch energy imports fell from 21% in 2021 to 3% in 2025 (CBS); the EU ban on Russian gas (new contracts from 18 Mar 2026, complete by end-2027) is in line with Dutch policy.

Russian LNG was about 4.4% of Portuguese LNG imports in 2024 and 7% of Sines discharges in 2025 (three Russian cargoes); the environment minister says Portugal is 'practically independent' of Russian gas and wants to cut the rest.

About a third of Russia's seaborne oil leaves the Baltic through the Danish straits: 292 transits by sanctioned tankers were logged in 2025, Denmark inspects at Skagen since Feb 2025 and NATO's Baltic Sentry watches the lane. The shadow fleet (500-1,300 vessels by the various counts, 632 listed by the EU) is the artery, and Denmark holds the tourniquet.

The Gazprom-Naftogaz transit contract of 2019 expired on 1 Jan 2025 and Russian gas stopped crossing Ukraine (about 14.3 bcm in 2024), ending the income and the leverage; Slovakia and Moldova (Transnistria) were the affected customers.

All crude reaching Serbia's Pancevo refinery goes through Croatia's JANAF pipeline, the sole route (mirrors Serbia's energy_import row). After US sanctions on NIS took effect in October 2025 deliveries stopped, the refinery shut on 2 Dec 2025 and restarted on 16 Jan 2026 under an OFAC licence now extended to 30 Oct 2026; JANAF's transport contract with NIS runs to 31 Dec 2026.
NIS is about 30% of JANAF's revenue, so the pipeline's dependence on Serbian crude volumes is the mirror of Serbia's dependence on the pipeline.
All imported crude reaches Pančevo through Croatia's JANAF pipeline, the sole route; NIS is about 30% of JANAF's revenue.

Moldova stopped buying gas from Gazprom in late 2023 (energy minister, 2 Oct 2023) and Gazprom halted all supply on 1 Jan 2025 when Ukrainian transit ended, citing Moldovagaz's debt. Chișinău-controlled Moldova now buys European gas; Russian gas reaches Transnistria only through intermediaries.

levers.summary: The government's crude exports have been blocked since the Houthi drone attacks on the Nushayma (18-19 Oct 2022) and Dabba (21 Oct 2022) terminals; the World Bank's Spring 2026 monitor says oil exports are still blocked. Volumes cannot be stated: they are zero.

The United States ended all USAID programmes in Afghanistan in 2025 after a January review (SIGAR: USD 765m humanitarian and about USD 1bn basic services cut, two small education programmes excepted); the State Department cited at least USD 11m in food aid siphoned to the Taliban. The Afghan economy lost its largest external grant donor.

Raiffeisen Bank International still owns Raiffeisenbank Russia, whose loan book fell from EUR 13.7bn to EUR 4.5bn since the invasion (ECB demanded a 65% cut by 2026); its Russian subsidiary lost EUR 118m in nine months of 2025 and a Russian court froze 100% of its shares in January 2025. RBI's 2025 profit excluding Russia was EUR 1.443bn.

Euroclear in Brussels holds about EUR 185bn of the EUR 210bn of Russian central-bank assets immobilised in the EU (the rest sits in private banks); the Council froze them indefinitely on 12 Dec 2025 under Article 122 by qualified majority. The depository passes the windfall profit to Ukraine and pays Belgian tax on it. Figures differ by source (EUR 180-193bn at Euroclear).

About EUR 185bn of the Bank of Russia's EUR 210bn immobilised in the EU sits at Euroclear in Brussels, frozen indefinitely by qualified majority since 12 Dec 2025; the windfall profit goes to Ukraine and the reparations-loan plan, blocked by Belgium in Dec 2025, was revived in Aug 2026 without a decision. Figures differ by source (EUR 180-193bn).
Serbia was the largest source of FDI in January-October 2025 (EUR 112.05m), just ahead of Turkey (EUR 110.88m).

The United States took 11.1% of China's USD 4.75tn of exports in 2025, down from the pre-war share: shipments to the US fell about 33% in August 2025 under the tariffs while the overall surplus rose about 20% to a record USD 1.19tn, redirected to ASEAN, Africa and Latin America. The market Beijing can least replace is the one it has depended on least since 2025.
US tariff on Myanmar's exports of 40% from July 2025 (set at 44% in April, revised to 40%); the junta asked for 10-20%.

US goods trade with China was an estimated USD 414.6bn in 2025 with a deficit of USD 202.7bn, down 31.8% (USTR); from Beijing's side the US took 11.1% of China's USD 4.75tn of exports in 2025 (Chinese customs), after shipments to the US fell about a third in August 2025 under the tariff wall.

The US took 7.1% of South African exports in 2025, down from 7.7% in 2024 and 7.9% in 2010, and fell from second to third place as a destination; vehicles and transport equipment were hit hardest by the 25% tariff of April 2025 and the 30% reciprocal tariff of August 2025. BNP Paribas gives 7.5% for a later 2025 window (vehicles 22% of exports to the US in 2024, farm goods 7%); the SARB figure is used (official basis wins).

China is India's top trading partner, with USD 131.6bn of imports and USD 19.5bn of exports in FY2025-26, a record deficit of USD 112bn (USD 99.2bn the year before); China supplied nearly 30% of India's fertilisers and in 2025 curbed rare-earth magnets and specialty fertilisers before easing after Wang Yi's August 2025 visit.
China supplied 23.6% of Japan's imports in 2025 (about USD 171bn of about USD 725bn), the largest single source; shipments to mainland China fell 0.4% in 2025.
Japan depended on China for 63% of its rare-earth imports in 2024 (CNN's calculation from trade statistics), the exposure that China's dual-use ban of Jan 2026 targets.

China is the first source of imports, 28.6% of the total in 2025 (the top since 2013), and the fourth export market at about 11%; PSA-based bilateral trade of USD 47.75bn left a Philippine deficit of USD 29bn. Chinese customs report a much larger total (USD 71.6bn for 2024), so the two series are not comparable.

Chinese visitors were 19,060 of 57,370 international arrivals in January to October 2025 (about 33%, computed here), up 25% and back at the top market after halving in 2024 (AP put China at about 30% of tourists then). Tourism is a services export and the vocabulary has no tourism type, so it is filed under trade_share. The tourism share of GDP is about 40% (AP) against more than half (RNZ, 2024): the atlas uses AP and does not reconcile the two.
China and Hong Kong, once Taiwan's first export market, fell behind the US in 2025: in the record month of May 2025 they took USD 14.06bn against USD 15.52bn for the US.

Russian fertiliser, which came by rail through Vainikkala after the border closure, covered 10-15% of the Finnish market; Russian rail tariffs rose eightfold on 1 Jul 2026, making rail imports unviable. The emergency supply agency says supply for the growing season is secured.

Latvian exports to Russia were EUR 962.5m in 2025 (4.9% of EUR 19.54bn), down 7.3%, led by prepared foodstuffs and beverages; imports from Russia fell 68.2% to EUR 125.6m (0.5% of imports). Imports from Russia and Belarus together fell from EUR 2.13bn in 2022 to EUR 193m in 2025.

Everything Hamas governs depends on what Israel lets in: about 227 aid trucks a day reach Gaza in Oct 2026 against a target of 600 in the plan, and Israel classes items such as tents and ventilators as dual use. Israel also withholds Palestinian tax revenues.

grand_strategy.reading:
Afghanistan under the Taliban is the pariah that outlasts its isolators.
The Emirate has no allies, no UN seat and a ruling circle indicted by the
ICC, and yet by October 2026 it is courted by Moscow (recognition, a
military-technical agreement), Beijing, Delhi, Riyadh, Doha and even
Brussels and Berlin. Luttwak's lamp shows why: it is useful against worse
enemies (the Islamic State in Khorasan) and it holds what everybody needs
(transit, water, minerals, a land bridge between Central and South Asia),
so each power that would isolate it has a competing reason to deal with it.
The strategy is to sell access without surrendering the social order,
which is why Zelin calls it recognition without concessions.
The weakness is the relation that used to protect it. The Pakistani
patron became the main military enemy over the TTP, and the paradox is
Luttwakian in the pure sense: loyalty to the movement's sister
organisation costs the Emirate its border, its main port route and, in
February 2026, air raids on Kandahar itself. Kabul now builds a ring of

grand_strategy.reading:
Albania runs the strategy of a small state that has bet everything on being
the most useful and best-aligned partner of whoever matters, and on Edi Rama
as the man who makes that bet personal. Every relation in the card follows
from it: NATO and the American channel for security, the EU for the future,
Italy and the UK for the migration currency, the Gulf and the Kushners for
capital, Turkey for arms and religion, Kosovo for the nation. The Luttwak
pattern is that each source of leverage creates a counter-pressure that
lands on the same pillar. The EU path is only as fast as the rule of law
allows, which is the front where Rama fights his own prosecutors; the
Kosovo pact adds to Albania's security and to Serbia's rearmament; the
Trump channel brings the Board of Peace and the Sazan protests together.
In 2026 the EU front is moving (three chapters closed on 14 Jul, the
Commission calling Albania and Montenegro the closest candidates) while the
American front is cooling (the 2027 NATO summit dropped from the draft
text, 10% tariffs). Two signals that are not rows: Albania's own ministers
played down the US embassy's Iran warning of 1 Apr 2026, and Greek
diplomatic sources publicly distanced Athens from Rama's claim at Delphi
that a Hague referral was agreed. The test is whether the EU path survives
the collision between Rama's immunities draft and the benchmarks, with
Greece as a possible veto at the end.

grand_strategy.reading:
The UAE under Mohamed bin Zayed runs the grand strategy of a small, rich state that has chosen to buy depth rather than inherit it: money turns into ports, ports into
clients, clients into reach, and reach into a seat at every table. The 'little Sparta' reading fits the 2015-2025 years, when Abu Dhabi built a ring of bases, terminals and proxies from
Mukalla to Berbera to Benghazi and held down the Islamist wing of the Arab world. Luttwak's reversal came in two beats. First, the December 2025 - January 2026 collapse of the Yemeni
bridgehead under Saudi pressure and Somalia's cancellation of every deal showed that a network of clients is strong against the weak and fragile against a neighbour that can fly its
own aircraft. Second, the war that began on 28 February 2026 hit the other half of the model, the hub: the state that sold itself as the safest place in the Gulf took the largest share of Iranian fire,
lost more than 90% of its Jebel Ali traffic and found that its only real shield was the United States, tied to it by a commitment and no treaty. The response is a double move - a harder
line (secret strikes, Iron Dome from Israel, the OPEC exit, the Netanyahu visit of 27 September) and a wider hedge (China, India, France, a Syria in which Abu Dhabi now invests).
The Saudi question is the pivot: the July-September 2026 thaw (the Mansour visit) looks like a truce in a rivalry that continues on the Horn, Sudan and Yemen, not a settlement; the Houthi
attacks on Saudi airports in October 2026, which the UAE condemned in the strongest terms, give both a common enemy again. One signal that is not a row: the UAE did not sign the Arab-Islamic statement against Israel's
recognition of Somaliland (December 2025). The dataset still lists UAE membership of OPEC; it ended on 1 May 2026.

grand_strategy.reading:
Milei's Argentina trades strategic alignment for money: the USD 20bn US Treasury swap and the USD 20bn IMF programme keep the peso and the debt afloat, and the price is a trade deal with Washington, the Isaac Accords with Israel and loud alignment with Trump. The hedge is the China swap, renewed to 2031, and the grain trade Beijing buys, and the paradox is that the American rescue and the Chinese trade pull against each other. Within South America the Mercosur bloc and the friction with Lula limit how far Milei can go, while the Falklands claim stays alive in rhetoric without stopping the London relationship.

Update of 2026-10-16. Two things changed the picture. First, the swap was used and repaid (USD 2.5bn, January 2026), so the American lifeline is now more a political tie than a debt, while the IMF programme missed its reserves target and inflation is back above 33% a year; the money that bought the alignment is not yet buying stability at home. Second, the Falklands stopped being rhetoric: the September 2026 sanctions on Sea Lion, the 60 proceedings and the arbitration threat turn the claim into a live quarrel with London, with the Israeli investor and with the oil majors' compliance departments, at the moment Milei's approval fell to 34%. The neighbourhood has split: a right-of-centre arc (Chile, Peru, Colombia, Paraguay, Bolivia) is warm, Brazil and Mexico are not, and the Mercosur summit showed that Argentina wants a bloc it can leave in all but name. Where the card had Argentina as a client who pays in alignment, it is now a client who is spending the alignment on a cause of its own.

grand_strategy.reading:
Armenia is a state that lost its war in 2020, its enclave in 2023 and its
patron's guarantee in between, and is now trying to buy a settlement and a new
set of protectors with the only coin it has left: the use of its territory. The
strategy is unusually coherent for a small state - peace with Azerbaijan first,
then a transport role (TRIPP, the Turkish rail link, Iran), then the EU and the US
as insurance, with Russia kept in the tent by gas, the base and the EAEU until the
other pieces hold. That is Luttwak's logic of the weaker party, which survives by
making itself useful to several stronger ones at once.

The paradoxes all sit at the joints. The treaty needs a constitution the June 2026
majority could not deliver; the corridor that ends the blockade is an American-run
concession through its own south; the pivot from Russia is financed by trade with
Russia; the EU law raises the cost of the gas that keeps the lights on. The
domestic fight with the Church and Karapetyan is not a side show: it is the same
contest, because the people who would vote 'no' to the preamble are also the ones
Moscow courts. Pashinyan's election win shows the public chose the pivot over the
nostalgia, but not with the margin the strategy needs, which is why the next real
test is not Moscow or Baku but a referendum with no date.

In 2026 the United States answered that hedge with visa restrictions tied to the programme; the government's response has been to request a review and promise tighter residency rules, not to change its line. The card is thin on the UK, Ukraine and Gaza, and on current trade and tourism shares, because those sources were not available within the flash budget.

grand_strategy.reading: Australia is the ally that pays for a guarantor that may not come, and the regional order it is building is the insurance on that premium. Everything since 2023 reads as one move: lock the United States in with submarines, minerals and a statute that survived a Pentagon review (AUKUS, endorsed December 2025; the framework signed on 20 Oct 2025), while turning every neighbour into a treaty partner that screens out China - Papua New Guinea as a mutual-defence ally (2025), Fiji as the fourth ally (6 Jul 2026), vetoes in Nauru and Tuvalu, no foreign bases in Vanuatu, a treaty bid for the Solomon Islands, a security treaty with Indonesia. The Albanese government has a free hand to do this: re-elected in May 2025 with 94 of 150 seats, it faces an opposition that attacks it for weakness on China rather than for the direction. The Luttwakian pattern is in the gap between the two halves. The guarantee is bought at the price of entanglement (an Australian crew aboard the submarine that sank the Dena) and is still conditional (3.5% asked, a Taiwan pre-commitment reportedly asked for, a 10% tariff in April 2025, a five-month review of the flagship programme), while the insurance is built by buying sovereignty from the very islands it is meant to protect, who answer by bargaining. Two signals that are not rows: Albanese's first reply to the Tasman drills was to stress that China had complied with international law, and the New Delhi Quad meeting of May 2026 spoke of tolls in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, which points to the Iran war rather than the Taiwan Strait. The question for 2027 is whether the ring of treaties and the submarine timetable hold long enough to outlast the guarantor's moods; the first stress test is the Solomon Islands treaty, which a Solomon Islands minister floated for the end of 2026.

grand_strategy.reading: Austria is a middle-sized trading state that has made a security policy out of not having one, and the two things that held that bargain up - cheap Russian gas and a post-1989 buffer of friendly neighbours - are gone. The gas is gone by the company's own choice and the market's help (December 2024); the buffer is being rebuilt through the Slavkov format, the Magyar reset in Hungary, the Balkan enlargement file and a Germany that now agrees with Vienna on borders. Neutrality remains untouchable at 75% public support, so the Stocker government, squeezed by an FPÖ polling at 34-36%, does what the Cold War Austria did: it moves with the West in everything except the vocabulary (EU sanctions yes, weapons no; Sky Shield yes, NATO no; a 2% defence goal on paper and about 1.2% in the budget). The real strategic exposure is economic, not military: Germany for the market, the United States for the second-largest outlet, China for the deficit, and the Brenner for the lorries. The Russia file shows the paradox best: the espionage cases (Ott, the embassy antennas) are taken to court and the diplomats expelled, but Raiffeisen's Russian bank and its EUR 3.15bn claim keep one Austrian foot in Moscow. For the atlas, Austria is a partner of almost everyone and an ally of a few by treaty, and its grade toward each follows the structure (EU membership, trade, geography), not the declaration of neutrality.

grand_strategy.reading:
Azerbaijan runs the strategy of a state that won its central war and is
now converting a position of force into a durable order without a patron.
The 2023 recovery of Karabakh and the exodus of about 100,000 Armenians
closed the territorial question on the ground; what remains is to make
the settlement legal (the Armenian constitution, the treaty, TRIPP) and
to keep the rents that pay for it while oil declines. The method is
multi-vector balancing: a treaty alliance with Turkey, arms and oil with
Israel, jets from Pakistan, a charter with Washington, gas to Europe,
transit with China and Central Asia, and a managed truce with Russia
after the AZAL crisis. Luttwak's pattern shows in each: every success
attracts the counter-pressure that limits it. The Israeli link brought
Iranian drones, the American corridor puts Washington on Azerbaijan's
border with Armenia, the argument won against Moscow ended in a
settlement without punishment, and a regime that jails journalists is
trading the European Parliament for the European Commission. Two
signals that are not rows: Aliyev skipped the Moscow Victory Day
parade in May 2025, and in 2026 the contacts with Russia reported to
us run through a deputy prime minister and foreign ministers, with no
head-of-state meeting found; and the peace is still a text initialled
but unsigned while Azerbaijani fuel and Russian grain already cross
the old front line. The test of the next year is whether Baku lets
Armenia reach the referendum on its own terms or keeps raising the price of signing.

grand_strategy.reading:
Belgium is a small power whose geography made it a host: the seat of the European
institutions and of NATO, the port of Antwerp, and the Euroclear depository that
keeps the greater part of Russia's frozen reserves. Its grand strategy is the
strategy of a host that must stay useful to everyone who matters and exposed to
none of them. That works while the host's guests agree; in 2025-26 they stopped
agreeing, and the host has been made to choose in public. The Euroclear file is the
clearest case in Luttwak's terms: a defensive refusal, motivated by fear of
liability, which gave Belgium the opposite of what it wanted (the loss of
influence among partners, a Russian pressure campaign that no EU decision
has lifted, and an indefinite freezing it can no longer veto).

The second thread is a late and under-funded rearmament. The F-35 decision, the
NASAMS purchase and the French nuclear-deterrence opening all point the same way,
but the 2% is a floor and the 3.5% an unfunded promise, and the F-35 delivery
schedule holds back the F-16s promised to Kyiv. The third is the empire's
afterimage: in Congo, Rwanda and Burundi Belgium speaks with moral authority and
little leverage, and each time it has used the one (sanctions, a public stance)
it has paid in the other. Non-events matter here: Belgium sent one officer, not
troops, to Greenland (January 2026) and did not join the eight NATO states hit by
Trump's tariff threat; it signed the New York Declaration on Palestine and has not
yet signed the decree.

grand_strategy.reading:
Bangladesh is a state between two giants that, for fifteen years, exported its
dependence on one of them and has since 2024 been testing the other. Under
Hasina, security, the border, the water and the grid were handed to India in
exchange for regime protection - 'a blank cheque', as a Dhaka academic put it -
and the cost came due in the uprising of July-August 2024, when the same India
that had underwritten the government became the place where it fled. What
Dhaka has done since is textbook Luttwak at the level of grand strategy: it
converts its single point of leverage, Hasina's person, into a diplomatic
claim, and it widens its menu (Beijing for money and fighters, Islamabad for
a signal, Ankara and Tokyo for industry, Washington for the market) so that
India no longer sets the price. But each widening is paid in the currency India
controls - the Ganges in December, the Teesta, diesel, the 4,096 km border,
the land ports - and India has shown it will use it (April-June 2025). The
BNP government of February 2026 has so far kept both doors ajar: a reset of
tone with Delhi, a four-day state visit to Beijing, and a trade deal with
Washington that the Supreme Court unmade within eleven days. The year-end
tests are concrete and dated: the Ganges Water Treaty lapses in December, LDC
graduation takes effect on 24 November, Rooppur is meant to reach the grid, and
the first Rahman visit to India (set aside around the BRICS summit in New Delhi
in September) has not happened. Two signals that are not rows: Dhaka declined
India's BRICS invitation on the ground of how it was extended (through the
BIMSTEC chair), and India's high commissioner has said he expects the water
and trade questions to move 'once the prime minister visits'. The risk is
that a state which wants to be nobody's client ends up as the disputed ground
between three clients' views of it - India's fear of a China-Pakistan-
Bangladesh convergence at the Siliguri Corridor, China's wish for Mongla and
Teesta, America's wish to see Dhaka not buy arms from Beijing.

grand_strategy.reading:
Bulgaria's strategy is that of a small, poor, shrinking member of two clubs
that has just chosen a leader who sells distance from both while keeping the
benefits of each. The euro (1 Jan 2026), full Schengen (1 Jan 2025), the NATO
battlegroup, the F-16s and the Westinghouse fuel are the anchor and nobody in
power is seriously proposing to cut it; what moves is the margin. Rumen Radev,
elected on 19 April 2026 with a single-party majority, uses the one thing a
small state has inside the EU, the veto, on Patriarch Kirill, on Lukoil's
founder and on North Macedonia, and pays for it by leaving Ukraine's
coalition and freezing state arms aid, while the factories keep selling.
The Luttwakian pattern is plain: each gain in leverage (the veto, the special
manager at Burgas, the transit corridor, the defence industry) is bought
with a loss in trust among the same partners who guarantee the anchor, and
the paradox of the North Macedonia block shows the end of that road.

no sign of restoring dialogue with Moscow and on 14 Jul that it was 'too weak'
to help Ukraine, not turning toward Russia; the pivot is therefore toward
caution, not toward the Kremlin. The oligarch network of Peevski, Magnitsky-listed
by the US in June 2021, lost its place in government in April 2026, but the
underlying fragility (eight elections in five years, a cabinet toppled by a
budget in December 2025) has not yet been tested by a hard budget under Radev.
What to watch: the Lukoil licences (reported to run to the end of October 2026),
the 21st-package endgame, whether Skopje and Sofia talk again before the
Council's next enlargement report, and whether the 15-month BOTAS suspension
ends with a renegotiated or a litigated contract.

grand_strategy.reading:
Bosnia and Herzegovina has no single grand strategy, and a card that pretends it
has one would be wrong. The objectives above are those of the state-level
institutions as the Bosniak-led majority reads them: the Presidency member
Becirovic, the foreign minister Konakovic, the Constitutional and State Courts,
the Central Election Commission, the SDA/SDP/Troika parties. Two other agendas
sit inside the same state. The Republika Srpska leadership of Dodik's SNSD,
which has just won again, wants to hollow the state out - competences back to
the entity, the OHR gone, status defined in Washington and Moscow - and keeps
the Serb seat in the Presidency (Cvijanovic) to veto what it cannot win. The
HDZ BiH leadership of Covic, backed by Zagreb, wants an election law that stops
non-Croats from choosing the Croat member and has just obtained the seat
outright. The paradox of the whole card is that a state must defend its
existence against one of its own entities, with tools (the Bonn powers, EUFOR,
Security Council cover, the courts) that belong in part to others, in a year in
which the guarantors weakened - Schmidt resigned in May and no successor was
agreed by mid-July, the US lifted its sanctions and said it was done with
nation-building, Orban fell in April - while the electorate stayed home (42%).
Signals that are not rows: the 31 Oct 2026 Security Council vote on EUFOR (the
October 2025 renewal was 15-0, so the base case is renewal; Russia's line on the
OHR is the thing to watch), the identity of the next High Representative,
whether Hungary under Magyar keeps Orban's line toward Banja Luka, and whether
the new Presidency can still produce a majority on foreign-policy questions
after Komsic's seat goes to HDZ. Sarajevo's room for manoeuvre is real only
where the EU and the entity cannot veto it: the courts, memory politics and the
capacity to say no to Belgrade.

grand_strategy.reading:
Belarus runs the strategy of a regime that has no allies except the one that
can also swallow it. Every move is a trade of the same thin assets - territory,
prisoners, potash, nuclear hosting, the capacity to make trouble at the
border - for survival, and the Luttwak pattern is that each trade sells a part
of the autonomy it was meant to protect: protection from Russia is bought with
the right to decide on launchers and on succession, and the hybrid pressure on
Poland and Lithuania, meant to be a lever, has closed the doors Minsk wanted
to sell (transit, rail, Klaipeda). Since September 2025 Lukashenko has found a
second buyer in Trump's Washington, which pays in sanctions relief for batches
of prisoners and which neither Moscow nor Brussels can yet outbid; the question
for 2026-27 is whether the American channel (embassy, Lukashenko's possible US
trip, a potash deal) is a real exit from Moscow's orbit or only a premium on the
old rent. The evidence says the second: the Oct 2026 statements promise 'full
support' to Putin, the Oreshnik is on duty, mobilisation is under way and the
EU wall stands until February 2027. Two signals that are not rows: Lukashenko's
remark that he has 'my own understanding' of the Ukraine war (2 Oct 2026), and
the unanswered succession question - no heir has been designated, the minimum
age for the presidency was raised, and the treaty's clause on mutual support for the constitutional order gives Moscow a say
in how it will be answered.

grand_strategy.reading:
Rodrigo Paz, in office since 8 November 2025, is trying to end the MAS era by buying
his way out of the fuel and dollar crisis: re-normalising relations with the United
States, reviewing the Chinese and Russian lithium contracts, and accepting a sea claim
that is closed in law, which keeps Chile a rival rather than an enemy. The real
constraint is the balance sheet, not the alignment: the lithium and gas that could
repay the debt are slow to monetise, and Washington's fuel and loans come at the price
of a sovereignty signal that the country built carefully since 2008. Not written in
this pass: the 2025-26 terms with Argentina, Brazil, Peru (the Ilo port) and Iran (the
2023 agreement), for which no source was read.

grand_strategy.reading:
Brazil plays the strategy of a continental power that will not take sides. It sells soybeans and beef to China, trades with the EU, speaks for the Global South in the BRICS and wants to lead on the Amazon, while US tariffs and sanctions and Argentina's feud push it to lean on its own bloc. The 25 October runoff is the constraint that decides how long this holds, because the sovereignty line that works against Washington is also the line that the Bolsonaro camp contests. Brazil's partners are many and none is a bloc of its own, so its room is the room that the vote leaves.

Enriched 2026-10-16 (protagonist pass). Read through Luttwak, Brazil is a country whose paradoxes all come from one fact: it is strong enough to be courted by every pole and too weak in arms to be feared by any. Each coercion has found it a substitute (China for the US soybean trade, the EU and Japan through Mercosur for the US market, the forest fund for the money of the rich states), and each substitute has made a new dependency (China's beef duty, the Brussels court, Argentina's veto in the bloc). The seams are visible: Washington presses it with tariffs and a Section 301 duty while Berlin, Madrid, London and Tokyo court it as a supplier of minerals and a partner in governance; Beijing buys what it grows and taxes it when it grows too much. The neighbourhood has turned right (Argentina, Chile, Paraguay, Bolivia, now Colombia and Peru) just as Brasilia needs it most, which makes the 25 October runoff a hinge for the whole card: a Flavio Bolsonaro victory would put the sovereignty line against Washington, the BRICS posture and the Gaza line in question at once (our reading: the campaign coverage read does not set out either candidate's foreign policy), while a Lula victory keeps the card as it stands, with the neighbours cooler and the tariff in place. The runoff polls are tight and lean to Flavio (Datafolha, 6-7 October: 49% to 45%, margin 2 points).

grand_strategy.reading: Brunei is a small, rich sultanate whose economy rests on one resource, oil and gas, with LNG sold to Japan since 1972. Its strategy is defensive and borrowed: it keeps its Islamic-monarchic identity at home (the 2014 sharia penal code, stoning in force since 2019), buys its security abroad (a British garrison and Singapore's jungle camp), and buys diversification from outside (Hengyi, Chinese capital at Pulau Muara Besar). The sharia code is the price it has chosen to pay for legitimacy, and the boycott it drew is the cost. The Limbang claim against Malaysia stays dormant rather than pressed.

grand_strategy.reading:
Bhutan runs the strategy of a small state that has bought its security by
tying it to one neighbour and then spent the proceeds on its own autonomy:
the 2007 treaty removed the clause that made Thimphu take India's advice, but
the hydropower grid, the rupee peg and the Indian grants keep the arrangement
close to the old one. Its three open fronts are China (no relations, an
undelineated border, Doklam in 2017, villages since 2016 that Thimphu does not
contest in public), the outside world (a deliberately thin network, a
carbon-negative and GNH brand used as the voice in the UN and elsewhere) and its
own population, which is leaving for Australia and beyond. The 2024 election
returned Tshering Tobgay (PDP, 30 of 47 seats according to one report) as prime
minister from late January 2024. The Gelephu Mindfulness City, with its
Indian-funded rail link, is the bet: if it works, Bhutan gets a second economic
base besides hydropower and a new reason for young people to stay. If it does
not, it is one more Indian-built asset. Gaps not covered in this card: Ukraine and
Gaza positions, Thailand and Singapore, the Gulf, and the US 2025 contacts beyond
the 10% tariff.

grand_strategy.reading: Botswana's grand strategy is to turn diamond dependence into state control: a bigger stake in De Beers, a say over sales, and a budget that survives the slump, with Debswana carrying about 90% of national diamond sales. The lab-grown glut and the US tariff erode the value of that stake faster than negotiation can raise it, so Gaborone is reported to be settling for about 25% rather than the majority it wanted. South Africa is the partner it leans on (SACU, the rand, the ports); Namibia, Zimbabwe, the EU and the UK are not yet read from sources, and the card is thinner than its tier because the call budget ran out.

Bangui's strategy is regime survival through foreign guards: Russian advisers since 2018 and a Rwandan force since 2020 hold the capital and the state, while Touadera seeks a third term under a constitution changed in 2023. grand_strategy.reading:
Canada is a middle power whose security and market both point south, and whose largest partner is now its coercer. Ottawa answers with a deliberate turn to Europe, Britain, Asia and the Arctic while keeping NORAD, CUSMA and NATO, the frame it cannot afford to lose. The turn is transactional by design, from the China EV quota to the India uranium deal, and the grades say so: partner with most of them, reluctant only where the alignment is new. Every hedge that answers Washington also gives it a target, so the test is whether the annual CUSMA reviews stay talk or become the exit.

The enrichment of 16 October 2026 adds the second front. Canada builds a ladder of partnerships (Poland, Japan, Germany, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, China) and an industrial defence plan (the TKMS submarines, the Australian radar), yet the monthly trade data still point south, and the federation that has to deliver all this has just elected a sovereigntist government in Quebec and will vote in Alberta on 19 October. A paradox not written as a row, because no source states it: the Arctic that Canada arms itself to defend is opened by the warming that the Alberta-to-coast pipeline of rank 4 would feed. Signals that are not rows: the Supreme Court of the United States struck down the IEEPA tariffs in February 2026, which removed the 35% duty but not the sectoral ones, and Washington answered with Section 232, Section 122 and then Section 338, so the legal ground under the coercion keeps moving while its target stays the same.

grand_strategy.reading:
Chile under Kast is trying to turn its copper and lithium into a position it can hold between the United States and China, while it tightens the northern border as the proof that its security policy works. The balancing line is real but thin: the US coalition is joined with explicit limits, China is needed as a buyer, and the regional minerals pact with Argentina, Bolivia and Peru is the first sign that the neighbours can be partners on resources as well as on migration. The weak point is the border itself, whose results depend on the controls of Peru and Bolivia and on a Congress that has already rejected part of the plan.

The July 2026 surcharge shows the price of the first choice: the guarantor that Kast courted taxed about four tenths of his exports to it, spared the copper it needs, and asked for a rewrite of the free trade agreement and for rules against China, while the buyer took 43.7% of the copper and was received a day later. The same logic runs in the lithium (a state-led partnership inherited from Boric and kept by a government that wants private capital) and in the south (the courtesy to Milei on the Malvinas became a question about Magallanes and the Antarctic). Chile's real strategy is the width of its trade treaties (the US, the EU, Japan, Korea, Mercosur) and the metal itself; what it lacks is a way to make either great power pay for its choices.

grand_strategy.reading:
China in October 2026 is the case Luttwak wrote the book about, read from the inside.
At the technical level the instruments are the best in the world and growing: the
largest navy by hulls, a third carrier, a coast guard with a licence to fire, a
monopoly on the magnets everyone's motors need, a trade surplus of USD 1.2 trillion.
At the level of theatre strategy the record is mixed by design: the Taiwan Strait is
rehearsed twice a year and never crossed, the shoals are taken by water cannon and
nature reserves rather than by landings, the Senkakus are visited 357 days a year.
At the level of grand strategy the paradox Luttwak predicted is visible in every
file of this atlas: Japan calls China its greatest challenge, fourteen states
reaffirm an award Beijing calls null, the EU keeps 'systemic rival', and the one
rival that matters, the United States, had to be bought into three truces with the
rare-earth lever that each truce spends. What is new in 2025-26 is that Beijing
appears to have read the logic: the thaws with India, Australia, South Korea,
Britain, Vietnam and even Brussels are a great state lowering its weight on the
scale, and the handling of Trump - hospitality, soybeans, a Board of Trade, 'healthy
competition kept within bounds' - is relational manoeuvre of a high order. What is
old is the reflex: one sentence from Takaichi brought back the whole arsenal of
coercion against the neighbour whose rearmament costs China most, and the
Philippine shoals got batons in the same summer. The constraints are heavier than
the rhetoric admits - deflation, 7.9 million births, a purged high command, a strait
it does not control and a chip embargo it cannot answer in kind - and they are why
the squeeze stays short of war. Three signals that are not rows: Beijing has let the
Power of Siberia 2 price wait for over a year, the measure of who is senior; it
asked Tehran, not Washington, to reopen Hormuz; and it made its best offer to Trump
on Taiwan not with a threat but with a request. The question the card leaves open
is Luttwak's own: whether a state can keep learning the logic of strategy faster
than its own weight teaches the others.

grand_strategy.reading: Kinshasa has lost its two largest eastern cities to a rebellion that its neighbour backs, and it cannot retake them alone, so it has spent 2025-2026 buying partners: Burundian troops in South Kivu, Ugandan operations against the ADF, Qatar's Doha track, Washington's minerals-for-security deal and an Angolan mediation that has come and gone. Every track gives it a seat and gives its enemies one too, which is why the strategy works by keeping the initiative with others rather than by winning on the ground. The minerals are the currency of the whole effort and the reason the outside powers are present, with China already holding most of the cobalt through Sicomines and the United States now seeking access. The 2028 succession has moved the decisive contest from the eastern front to the capital, where the Catholic bishops and the opposition are the only national forces able to stop a third term, and that is the constraint no foreign mediator can remove.

grand_strategy.reading: Sassou Nguesso's aim is to keep the system he has run for decades in power to 2031, and the oil income that pays for it is also the tightest constraint: more than 80% of export revenue against debt near 98% of GDP. He plays the great powers against each other for money and cover, Paris for aid and a long tie that also carries its own legal exposure over the family's assets, Beijing as oil buyer and creditor, and Moscow for the 2024 pipeline, and none of them is a treaty patron. The test of the next years is whether the refinancing buys enough time for oil to hold its price, and the paradox is that the buyer who funds the state is also a creditor whose claims it must manage.

grand_strategy.reading:
Colombia changed its partner in 2026 without changing its problem: the cocaine economy and the armed groups on the Venezuelan border are the same, and a hard-line Trump ally sworn in on 7 Aug 2026 has bet that Washington's force can do what negotiation did not. The reset reverses the Petro-era rupture (decertification, sanctions on the president, the tariff war with Ecuador), and the energy lever is back in use, while the Belt and Road pact of May 2025 is a non-binding letter that the new government has not yet addressed in any source found. The paradox is that the rupture cost Colombia its aid and its standing, and the reset buys security cooperation at a price that the policy itself may push across the borders, into Venezuela and Ecuador (an inference, not yet sourced).

Added on 16 Oct 2026, after ten weeks of the new government. The reset has two faces. At home, it replaces negotiation with force (four air strikes since 7 Aug, an ultimatum to the Clan del Golfo, extradition and surrender as the exits) and bets that Washington's backing will outlast a 49.66% mandate and a minority in Congress. Abroad, it prices alignment in ideological currency: Israel restored and its embassy moved to Jerusalem, Cuba and Nicaragua cut, the Sahrawi Republic frozen, South Africa's ICJ case abandoned, the Palestine vote abstained, 14 embassies closed. The payoff so far is thin and probationary: a waiver instead of recertification on 16 Sep, Petro still on the SDN list on 7 Oct, and a Venezuela that Washington took off the list while Colombia stayed on it. The test comes within a year, when the coca hectares of 2025 and 2026 will be counted against a promise that supply can be cut by force, and the 2024 data (a 54% fall in forced eradication with the smallest rise in coca area in four years) do not yet say it can. What the new government's line on China, Russia and the Belt and Road letter of May 2025 will be remains unsourced; so does the status of the ELN's Venezuelan sanctuary after the change of government.

grand_strategy.reading: Cuba's strategy is to outlast the fuel blockade without changing its political order, and it keeps every channel open, from a Russian tanker and Vietnamese rice to a Mexican offer and Vatican mediation, while refusing to negotiate the system itself. Its means are thin: tourism run by foreign chains and a few diplomatic channels, against a US that has turned the fuel supply itself into the lever. The paradox is structural: the pressure meant to make Havana bend works through its suppliers, so each partner who hesitates leaves the grid darker and pushes more Cubans out.

grand_strategy.reading:
Cyprus runs the grand strategy of a small member state of the EU that is also half
an occupied island: it cannot change facts on the ground, so it multiplies the
number of actors whose interests are tied to the island and hopes that one of them
will, in the end, move Turkey. The EU is the main multiplier (membership, the
presidency, the veto on SAFE and the customs union), the Greek-French-Israeli-US
ring is the second (air defence, arms, drills), gas is the third (Egypt, Israel,
Greece, Chevron, Eni). Each of them works, and each of them has a Luttwak cost:
the veto gives Ankara a grievance, the ring gives it a pretext, the gas makes
Cyprus a client of Cairo and Jerusalem, and the bases that tie Britain and the
United States to the island are the ones that drew Iranian-made drones onto it on
1-4 March 2026. The year's two facts pull in opposite directions: the election of
Erhurman (19 Oct 2025, 62.8%) and a UN track that is moving, against a Turkey that
is more entrenched in the EU's defence and trade files and a Gaza-and-Iran war
that has made Cyprus a front-line state. Two signals that are not rows: Guterres
leaves office on 31 Dec 2026, so Nicosia has a deadline it did not set, and the
president's own praise for Trump ('you know where you stand') comes with a defence
budget cut at home. The north is not an actor in the atlas: it is recorded through
Turkey's stance, rows and troop presence, not as a territory with its own grade.

grand_strategy.reading:
Czechia in 2026 runs two foreign policies out of one state. The government
of Andrej Babiš (ANO with the SPD and the Motorists, in office since December
2025) wants a cheaper, more domestic and more bilateral Czech Republic: no
Czech money for Ukraine, no migration pact relocation, no Green Deal, a
cautious opening to Beijing and a warm one to Jerusalem. The president, Petr
Pavel, the intelligence services and most of the arms industry keep the older
line: Russia as the threat, NATO and Berlin as the frame, Ukraine's war as
Czechia's own. Luttwak's pattern is the squeeze between them: each saving
made for the voter (the ammunition channel left unfunded, defence at 1.8%,
the opt-out from the EU loan) erodes a lever that Prague needs elsewhere -
leverage in Berlin and Washington, credibility in NATO, goodwill in Brussels
that the Dukovany loan will need before the end of 2026. What has not
changed is the structure: Russian oil and gas are out, the Korean nuclear
build is under way, Germany still takes a third of exports, and every
hostile act from Moscow (the BIS warnings, the September 2026 reciprocal
measures) pushes the cabinet back toward the line it ran against. Two signals
that are not rows: Babiš said in March 2026 that he was not planning a White
House visit and that the EU is 'always the most important'; and Pavel's
own suggestion in June 2026 that Czechia should drop the koruna for the
euro if it holds the country back, which the cabinet (which dropped the
annual euro-readiness report) will not follow.

grand_strategy.reading: Germany is a trading state that has to become a military power without having the people, the habits or the political consensus for it. Its grand strategy since 2022 is to buy security from three directions at once: from itself (the debt-brake carve-out and a Bundeswehr meant to be the strongest conventional force in Europe), from Washington (nuclear sharing, Patriot, F-35, and the hope that the troop drawdown stops at 5,000) and from a Europe it tries to organise around Paris and Warsaw. Each channel undermines another: autonomy hastens American retreat, American purchases weaken the Franco-German industrial project, spending outruns recruitment, and the domestic price, an AfD that wins eastern states while the centre governs with a thin majority, limits how much of this the electorate will fund. Its handling of Russia is the clearest part: Moscow is the declared 'greatest threat', hybrid attacks are treated as such, aid to Ukraine is the largest in Europe but stops short of Taurus and of troops. Toward China, Israel and Turkey the same Germany behaves less like a leader than like an exporter with a guilty conscience: de-risking is proclaimed and the trade deficit grows, Staatsraeson is proclaimed and then conditioned, a difficult NATO partner becomes the bet in the eastern Mediterranean. The pattern a Luttwak reader would flag is that Berlin's choices are rational one by one and self-defeating together; the test of 2027 is whether the Lithuania brigade, the F-35s and the budget become forces in being before the American drawdown and the AfD set the terms.

grand_strategy.reading: Denmark is a small state whose grand strategy has been reduced, since January 2025, to one question: how to stay in the American security system while an American president claims part of its territory. The Danish answer has three layers. Keep the formal position unmovable (sovereignty over Greenland and the Faroes, self-determination for Greenlanders), pay the price in usable goods (bases, F-35s, an Arctic build-up of tens of billions of kroner), and move the quarrel into NATO and Europe, where Rutte and the European leaders can absorb it. The 22 September 2026 trilateral agreement shows the method working and its cost: the crisis is calmer, the Kingdom's flag still flies, and both sides publish opposite readings of the same text. Behind the Greenland file stands the second pillar, which is Russia: a country that sits on the Baltic's only exit, takes the hybrid blows (drones over airports, flares at a helicopter, cables) and is both one of Ukraine's leading European donors (the Kiel tracker names it, with the Netherlands, right behind Germany for May-June 2026) and a builder of a European floor under NATO. The weakness is domestic and structural: a minority coalition, a Greenland that is no longer a colony to be spoken for, and an export economy that lives on American and German markets. The grades on this card follow the structure: the United States is a reluctant ally (a treaty ally with an open grievance, not a rival), Russia a rival (not an adversary, because Denmark seeks Moscow's restraint rather than its fall), China a reluctant partner.

grand_strategy.reading: Algeria runs the grand strategy of a rentier state whose army is the regime and whose two standing antagonists, Morocco and France, are the two neighbours it cannot choose: one across a border closed since 1994, the other across a sea that carries its gas, its diaspora and its memory. The 1962 identity of anti-colonial sovereignty, the Sahrawi referendum and the colonisation law substitute for the votes it does not get (46.1% disputed in 2024, about 21% in 2026), so every rupture is domestic currency as much as foreign policy. The paradoxical logic shows at each step: the tap that was meant to punish (the Maghreb pipeline, Spain in 2022) was also the only income, so it ran on; each door shut (Morocco, the UAE, France's embassy premises, Mali's airspace) removes a seat at the table where Washington, Paris and Rabat then decide without Algiers. Two signals that are not rows: Algiers did not vote on Resolution 2797 and has not answered the US push for talks with Rabat, and the chief of staff's reported absence from the December 2025 council on a term-extending revision (Yabiladi, single source) is a possible seam inside the regime. The thaws of 2026 (Spain, Mali, France) are not reconciliation; they are the rentier state discovering that its leverage is bounded by its customers. Grading note: Morocco stays a rival, not an adversary, by the ontology's own test: the aim Algiers declares is Sahrawi self-determination and security, not Moroccan defeat, and the Kabylie charge is the nearest it comes to an existential accusation.

grand_strategy.reading:
Egypt is a state that sells its position. It cannot feed, fuel or finance itself,
so the strategy of the Sisi regime is to be too central to be allowed to fail:
the Suez Canal and the Rafah crossing, the Gaza table, the Arab League seat,
a Mediterranean liquefaction hub, an army that can be lent to the Gulf. Each
of the payers is a different patron (the IMF and the EU for the
balance sheet, the Gulf for cash, Washington for the army, Paris and Berlin for
the equipment, Moscow for the nuclear plant, Beijing for industry) and the cost
is that none of them is aligned with the others on Sudan, Israel or Iran. The year
2026 widened every gap at once: the US-Iran war doubled the energy bill and put
Egyptian jets on Emirati soil while Cairo called itself neutral; the Israeli gas
that was meant to be the bridge is the lever Jerusalem uses against the Sinai
buildup; the Houthis, not Egypt, decide whether the canal pays; and the Nile has
turned from a water dispute into a Horn-wide alliance contest with Ethiopia in civil
war. The Luttwak reading is that Egypt's moves are rational at each level and
self-defeating across levels: tactical gains (a summit, a deposit, a contract) are
paid for by a strategic dependency that will be called in when the IMF programme
ends in December 2026. Gaps in this card: Jordan, Iraq, India, the UK, Djibouti, and
the status of Tiran and Sanafir were not researched (no source retrieved).

grand_strategy.reading: Eritrea runs the strategy of a garrison state that has turned isolation into method: an army with no end date, a constitution never applied, and a ring of partners (Egypt, Somalia, Sudan, with Russia at the UN) built to keep Ethiopia off the Red Sea. The structural problem is that it holds the coast and the port that Ethiopia wants, so each Ethiopian move on Assab reads in Asmara as an attack, and each Eritrean move in Tigray reads in Addis as an invasion. grand_strategy.reading:
Spain's grand strategy is the strategy of a middle power that has chosen to be
ruled by its law and its domestic coalition rather than by its geography, and
geography is now collecting. Madrid's south is a border with a monarchy it
cannot afford to quarrel with and a gas pipeline from a republic that cannot
be ignored; its east is an energy island; its west an ally; its north a
grudging partner (France) and a flat refusal of the Atlantic bill (2.1%
against 5%). The Sanchez government answered each pressure with a legal
gesture (the Sahara letter of 2022, Palestine in 2024, the arms embargo of
2025, the bases refusal of 2026, regularisation), which won votes and
moral standing but accumulated debts: Trump now names Spain as the outlier,
Israel and Spain have downgraded embassies, Morocco reopened Ceuta and
Melilla in August 2026 after a mass crossing, Italy suspended Schengen
arrangements for a month. The Luttwak reading is that the gestures were
cheap while the system was friendly, and became expensive when friction
arrived in a pile - Iran war, Ceuta, NATO summit, Trump, an election. Two
signals that are not rows: the government itself justifies the 2.1% line by the welfare
state and public finances, so it is a domestic bargain as much as a
strategy, and the snap election of 29 Nov 2026 makes every position here
provisional: polls point to a PP-led government with Vox, whose foreign
line on Gaza, Iran and Latin America would likely differ.

grand_strategy.reading: Estonia runs the grand strategy of a front-line state that has decided to spend its way to being un-attackable rather than hope for a guarantor: 5.43% of GDP, a fortified border, a deep-strike arsenal and a dense net of partners (UK, Finland, Poland, Germany, Korea) around an American umbrella it publicly trusts and privately hedges. The Luttwak pattern is that each hardening has a cost that returns on the same front: the forward posture raises exposure, enforcement at sea shows the limits of the law, grid independence concentrates risk in cables, and the defence of the nation-state against Russian leverage on the minority hands Moscow a grievance narrative. Russia is graded a rival, not an adversary: Estonia seeks deterrence, a Russian defeat in Ukraine and a Russia that pays, not the end of the Russian state, and keeps an embassy and a border regime open. The Kremlin's line that Russia 'poses no threat' to Estonia and the Estonian intelligence judgement that Moscow has no intention of attacking in the coming year are signals, not rows: both sides are reading the other's limits. The open question for 2027 is the American presence after the end-2026 rotation and an election that a weak coalition may lose.

grand_strategy.reading:
Ethiopia is Luttwak's landlocked power that named its sea access a right and, by naming it, summoned the Red Sea coalition against itself. Abiy's strategy rests on one national project, the GERD, and one national claim, an outlet to the sea; both are legitimate to Addis Ababa and both are read abroad as a threat. The Nile gave Egypt a motive; the sea claim gave Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan a common text (El Alamein, 4 Oct 2026); and the one war Abiy cannot afford, the internal one, gave Eritrea and Egypt a way to hurt him that no treaty forbids. The pattern is the paradox of success in strategy: each win (the dam built, the election won, Mekelle retaken after the TPLF withdrew) raised the price the neighbours would pay to stop the next.

Signals that are not rows. Abiy swore the oath on 5 Oct 2026 and repeated the sea claim the day after the Alamein summit, so the speech was an answer, not a plan; he softened it by 'give and take' and by the March 2026 pledge of no bullet at Eritrea, Somalia, Djibouti or Kenya, but the UN letter of 8-9 Oct invoked Article 51 against Eritrea and the diplomatic channel is closed since 1 Oct. Somalia sat at both tables within a week. Washington's July envoy tour took in Cairo, Mogadishu and Asmara, not Addis Ababa. Whether Eritrea is truly behind the alliance is Addis Ababa's allegation, unverified in the sources, and Cairo says it is 'a domestic crisis'. The Pretoria agreement, signed by Addis Ababa and the TPLF but not by Eritrea, is now the document everyone cites and nobody observes. Open question: does the dam, the election and the war on four fronts leave the army enough force to take a port, or only enough to threaten one - and is the threat itself what will keep the ring closed?

grand_strategy.reading:
Finland runs the strategy of a frontline state that has finally been given the
alliance it avoided for seventy years, and now has to make it real before the
patron's attention drifts. The aim is not to defeat Russia but to be an
unprofitable target: a large reserve army, American aircraft and basing,
Swedish and Nordic depth, a sealed border, and a loud insistence that Ukraine
must not lose. The grade for Russia is therefore rival, not adversary - the
government says it is not an enemy, aims at weakening Russian capacity through
sanctions and deterrence, and keeps the door open to dialogue after a ceasefire
- but the structure under it (Winter War memory, hybrid pressure, the longest
border) is hostile. The Luttwak pattern is that every layer of security adds
a new exposure: NATO membership brought instrumentalised migration, drones and
GNSS jamming; the Trump channel brought the Greenland tariff threat; the
border closure brought a Russian reply and an end to contact; the shadow-fleet
seizures ran into the law of the sea. Two signals that are not rows: Stubb's
habit of speaking both to Trump (golf, icebreakers) and of preparing Finns for
a post-war thaw with Russia, and the quiet extension of the defence memorandum
with Israel in the same years in which the president publicly condemned the
occupation. The open questions for 2027 are the election, whether the 3.2%
path survives the deficit, and whether the Eagle S case ends in a conviction
or in the Supreme Court.

Rabuka's Fiji takes the Pacific frame as its own instrument: it chairs the Melanesian
Spearhead Group, carried the Ocean of Peace through the Forum and opened an embassy in

grand_strategy.reading: France runs the strategy of a medium power with a first-rank vocabulary: nuclear, permanent seat, an army meant to be 'feared' (Macron, July 2025), and a claim that Europe must become sovereign. The pattern in Luttwak's terms is that each assertion of autonomy needs a partner it cannot dominate. The 2 March 2026 offer of forward deterrence needs Germany and Poland, who also want Washington; the Coalition of the Willing needs the United States for the ceasefire; the arms-export drive needs EU money that Mercosur and the deficit make harder to unite. Since 2022 the centre of gravity has moved north and east (Finland, Romania, Poland, Denmark, Greenland) as the African position collapsed, and the Mediterranean (Greece, Cyprus, Lebanon, Morocco) is the compensation. Two signals that are not rows: the 2027 election is the main unknown, with Macron the least popular president since 2017 and Marine Le Pen eligible and leading, so every commitment made in 2025-26 (Paris Declaration, nuclear talks, Greece pact) will be tested by a successor; and no French ambassador has been reported back in Algiers despite the thaw. The fiscal squeeze is the single constraint that touches every objective.

grand_strategy.reading:
The United Kingdom runs the grand strategy of a power that has lost the
weight to act alone and the habit of not acting, and has decided to make
itself the organiser of the coalitions in which others' weight is added to its
own: the Coalition of the Willing for Ukraine with France, the JEF in the
north, bilateral treaties with Berlin, Warsaw, Paris, Oslo and Canberra, and
a nuclear role it now coordinates with Paris while it rents the delivery
system from Washington. Luttwak's reversal is everywhere. The more the UK
organises, the more it needs the American umbrella it is trying to insure
against; the more it obeys international law toward Washington (Iran bases,
Caribbean intelligence) the less Washington obliges it (Chagos, the Falklands
hints, tariffs); the more it engages China and the EU for growth, the more the
security and political price rises at home. Underneath is a politics
that has not found its centre: 2026 saw the May rout, Starmer's fall on
22 June and Burnham's arrival on 20 July with a poll bounce that Reform had
erased in YouGov's last September poll. Three signals that are not rows: the postponement of the
July UK-EU summit until Brussels knew who would be in Downing Street; the
Healey resignation that turned the 3% question into a government-wide problem;
and Washington's 'neutrality' statement on the Falklands only after a leaked
Pentagon email suggested otherwise. For the next review: whether a UK-EU summit
in November-December fixes the SPS and youth texts, whether the Autumn Budget
funds the Defence Investment Plan, and whether Burnham's 'all options' survives
contact with a Reform lead.

grand_strategy.reading:
Georgia is run by a party that has decided its own survival, and a particular
idea of order, come before the country's formal strategy of Euro-Atlantic membership
(on paper still the constitutional line). Since the May 2024 foreign-influence law the
state has behaved as a hedging regime: it keeps every Western instrument it can without
paying the political price (candidate status, free trade, citizens' visa-free travel,
NATO contacts), keeps Russia calm (no sanctions, flights, trade, no talk of the
territories) and looks for other patrons (China, Turkey, Azerbaijan, the Gulf) and for a
different America. That is Luttwak's pattern of a move that works against its own end:
each step that protects power at home (the foreign-agents law, the arrests after
28 November 2024 and 4 October 2025, the party-ban case) lowers the value of the Western
shell that the economy rests on, and raises the weight of the one actor, Russia, whose
forces hold a fifth of the territory. Three signals that are not rows: the party ban was
widened to For Georgia in September-October 2026, a year after the first filing; Moscow
still says no dialogue without recognition of Abkhazia and South Ossetia; and a Hungarian
change of government in May 2026 reportedly removes the veto that protected Tbilisi from EU
sanctions. The Middle Corridor is the economic bet that holds the arrangement together:
cargo is up and the IMF sees 6.5% growth, but the corridor itself is not Georgia's to
secure, and its Western users are the ones being pushed away.

grand_strategy.reading: Greece runs the strategy of a status-quo power with a longer coast than its allies' attention. Its whole grand strategy is deterrence by alliance: the single threat is Turkey, the single legal case is the law of the sea, and the instruments are borrowed - French treaty text, American bases and aircraft, Israeli air defence, EU money, Egyptian and Cypriot signatures. Mitsotakis has chosen to run it on two tracks at once, a managed calm with Erdogan (Athens Declaration, Ankara summit, foreign-minister channel) and a quiet build-up of the ring around him, and the pattern Luttwak would recognise is that each track feeds the other: the calm gives Athens room to arm and plan its seas, the planning and the arms give Ankara reasons to legislate the Blue Homeland and decree parks. 2026 is the year in which the two tracks collided: the F-35 and CAATSA signals from Trump in Ankara, the marine parks of 15 August, the drone off Alexandroupolis, the Israeli contract of 31 August, and the renewed Franco-Greek defence agreement of 25 April, all within eight months of the Ankara summit. Signals that are not rows: Athens has not recognised Palestine ('at the right time'), the Greek foreign ministry's line on Piraeus is 'aligned with the US but will respect past agreements', and the Blue Homeland bill has been reported since spring but not confirmed as tabled. The domestic horizon is a spring 2027 election with the governing party near 30%, which pushes Mitsotakis toward visible firmness on the sea and toward the promise of calm on the ground.

grand_strategy.reading:
Croatia plays the strategy of a small state that has solved its existential
question - NATO and the EU - and is now spending the dividend. Its first
objective is no longer to be admitted but to make Serbia's rearmament and
its own memory politics the neighbour's problem: it deters from inside the
Alliance, speaks to Belgrade in the voice of a member state (conditionality
on the missing, a reported weapons purchase, a defence declaration with
Tirana and Pristina) and keeps the instruments that are not its own - the
US licence on JANAF, EU loans for tanks, the High Representative in
Sarajevo - within reach. The Luttwakian pattern is that every lever is
borrowed and every success invites the response it was meant to prevent:
deterrence feeds Serbian rearmament, a refusal to receive Vucic hands him
the memorial stage, discipline on Russian oil prices out a Hungarian
partner it needs for INA. Domestically the strategy has two authors:
Plenkovic, EU-centred, tied to a Homeland Movement coalition, and
Milanovic, re-elected with 74.9%, who vetoes deployments and cancels
summits; Belgrade reads the harder voice. Two signals that are not
rows: Orban's fall in April 2026 has changed the weather with Hungary
overnight, and Serbia's snap election of 25 October 2026 may reset a tone
that Zagreb has so far refused to reset. Bosnia, where Zagreb's kin are
a constituent people dependent on imposed rules, is the arena in which
its soft power is thinnest.

grand_strategy.reading: Hungary is a mid-sized state whose grand strategy for sixteen years was to extract rents from every patron at once - Russian gas and a Rosatom reactor, Chinese factories, Gulf and Azerbaijani deals, an American president's goodwill - while using the EU veto as the currency of that bargaining. The April 2026 election replaced that model with its opposite, and the transition is the real story of the card: Magyar's Hungary wants to be a normal member of NATO and the EU (money, trust, a V4 that talks to Poland again), yet it inherits every dependency the old model built. What has changed is the tone, the people and a dozen decisions already taken - the ICC exit reversed, Russian diplomats expelled, the veto on Ukraine's clusters lifted, funds unlocked, Chinese plants inspected. What has not changed is the structure underneath: Russian crude and gas still arrive, Paks II is under review but not cancelled, the Serbian partnership and MOL's NIS deal survive the change of leader, Fico remains Hungary's closest ally in the region, the border fence stays, and the old minority grievances are only being handled differently. Luttwak's logic bites hardest on the new government: every concession to Brussels spends a lever, every audit of an Orban-era deal risks the counterpart who keeps the lights on. The next tests are dated: the Council vote on funds (13 Oct), the US waiver (21 Nov), OFAC and NIS (30 Oct), and whether Netanyahu lands in Budapest on 23 Oct.

grand_strategy.reading:
Indonesia under Prabowo is the textbook hedger that has chosen to hedge at scale: it has not left the free-and-active line, it has made the line wide enough to hold a BRICS seat, a US defence partnership, a Russian oil contract, an Australian security treaty and Chinese jets at the same time. In Luttwak's terms this is relational manoeuvre rather than alliance: no seam is exploited, because Jakarta sits on all of them, and the point is to make itself too useful to be pushed to either side. The method works while the great powers are in low-grade competition and the bills fall due in different currencies; the Lowy analysis dates its limit to April 2026, when the Iran war closed Hormuz and made energy, not doctrine, decide the week.
The paradoxes are the price of belonging everywhere. Each club costs standing in another: BRICS cost a tariff threat in Washington, the Natuna formula cost the legal case against Beijing, the Board of Peace cost the street at home, the nickel ban cost leverage over its own smelters. The material limits are older than Prabowo: a 3% deficit cap that cannot carry free meals, a capital city and an arsenal at once; a net energy importer; a navy for an archipelago of thousands of islands. The archipelago is Indonesia's strength (everyone needs its straits) and its weakness (no one can be kept out of them).
The grades here follow structure, not courtesy. Almost every great-power relation is partner, because Indonesia treats all of them as purchasable, and the bonds say what the partnerships are worth: Saudi Arabia, Palestine and Malaysia are kin, Turkey and Papua New Guinea affinity, the others bought. Whether this is strategy or drift is the open question in the literature; this card records the structure (low confidence on trend after April 2026, since the Gaza deployment, the overflight request and the J-10 contract are all unresolved as of 12 Oct 2026).

grand_strategy.reading: India's grand strategy is relational manoeuvre among the great powers. In Luttwak's terms it is the strategy of a state strong enough to refuse a patron and not strong enough to ignore any of them: it extracts from each - US technology and defence frameworks, Russian oil and arms, Chinese inputs and a quiet border, European markets, Gulf energy and money, Japanese capital - by being too large to coerce and too useful to lose. The paradoxical logic is that each of these relations is also a pressure point, and the pressures are not independent. The week of 11-17 September 2026 shows the shape: Putin in Delhi on the 11th, Xi on the 12th, the US Congress passing a tariff authority on Russian oil buyers on the 17th. The culminating point of manoeuvre is reached when all three pull at once and the price of waiting - a tariff, a border incident, a sanction - overtakes the benefit of keeping options open; in July, with the Hormuz war on, Russian imports hit 2.8 million barrels a day just when Washington sought less of them, and the US-India trade agreement that would reward a shift remains unsigned. The Pakistan file is read here as rivalry, not mortal enmity: New Delhi's declared aim is deterrence of terrorism, with a reversible lever (the Indus treaty) and an accepted ceasefire, and it does not seek the end of the Pakistani state - which is what separates it from Israel and Iran. The neighbourhood is where the strategy is least comfortable: the instruments of primacy (credit lines, hydropower, refuge for Hasina) generate reactions that open space for China. Confidence in this reading is moderate: it rests on tier-3 press for most 2026 events, and several figures (Indonesian and Vietnamese BrahMos values, the Rafale and submarine contracts, the status of the US sanctions act) are unconfirmed.

grand_strategy.reading:
Iran in October 2026 runs the strategy of a regime that has lost the war it
prepared for and cannot afford to concede it. Between June 2025 and February
2026 its three layers of security collapsed one after another: the nuclear
sites, the proxy belt (Assad gone in December 2024, Hezbollah gutted) and
finally the leadership itself, when the US-Israeli campaign killed Ali Khamenei
and then Larijani. What is left is a system run by the Revolutionary Guards
behind an unseen successor, with the economy at near-zero oil income, a
population it shot at in January, and one lever: the Strait of Hormuz and the
ability to hit Gulf infrastructure. Luttwak's logic shows in how that lever
works against its owner: each use of it hardens an adversary (the UAE,
Qatar, Saudi Arabia) that Tehran needs as a neighbour, and each hedge it
builds (enriched uranium, the NPT-exit bill) justifies the next strike. The
great powers it counted on (Russia, China) offer words, oil purchases and
mediation, not defence, and both want Hormuz open more than they want Iran
to win. Two signals that are not rows: Mojtaba Khamenei has not been seen in
public since his appointment, and the Majlis has not yet voted on leaving the
NPT: the one move Tehran has not made is the one that would end the ambiguity.
The cards that matter are Washington's (whether it still wants regime change,
as Netanyahu does, or a deal on enrichment, as Vance's 7 October language on a
'meaningful reduction' suggests) and Beijing's (whether it will trade its
oil dependence for pressure on Tehran).
