grand_strategy.reading:
Iraq in October 2026 is a state whose grand strategy is to be nobody's
battlefield and nobody's client while owning too little force and selling
one product through one closed strait. Its means are access and contracts
(oil for Chinese pipelines, French gas, American majors, Turkish water
works) and its currency is the promise that every patron will be paid
from the same barrels. The Luttwakian pattern is that each safeguard
creates the next exposure: ending the coalition earns sovereignty and
removes the pressure that held the factions; the PMF is state-funded and
so brings foreign strikes on the state; the escape from Hormuz runs
through Turkey, Syria and Kurdistan; the Khor Abdullah claim spent Gulf
goodwill just before the Gulf was needed. The balance with Iran is
structural, not chosen: Iranian gas and the Shia parties tie Baghdad to
Tehran even as the war cut the gas and Iranian drones hit Erbil. Signals
that are not rows: the militias' 'victory' on 30 September is a
statement, not yet an attack; Maliki was stopped by a public American
warning, not by a parliamentary vote; and the date that matters, 30 June
2027, belongs to a government that has filled only part of its cabinet.
Open gaps in this pass: Jordan and Egypt (the triangle), the Gulf grid,
Saudi Arar and the electricity link, Russian arms, the EU, Germany,
water with Iran and the Shatt al-Arab.

grand_strategy.reading:
Israel in October 2026 runs the strategy of a state that has won every
battle it chose since 7 October 2023 and cannot convert any of them into an end
state. Its method is preventive, decapitating force within a patron's shadow:
the Twelve-Day War, the killing of Nasrallah, the Doha strike and the war on
Iran from 28 February 2026 weakened Iran and its allies as an organised threat, and the
buffer zones in Gaza (about 60%), Lebanon (about 65 villages) and Syria (nine
posts) are meant to make that victory permanent. Luttwak's paradox is that each
instrument of success spoils its sequel: the decapitations leave movements with a
motive and no ceiling, the buffer zones prevent the stabilisation force, the
Lebanon-for-disarmament framework and the Syria talks that would let the army
leave, and the settlement drive moves toward the annexation red lines of the
Emirates, Jordan and Egypt and so away from the Saudi normalisation that would
end the isolation. The relation that governs all the others is the American one:
Israel needs Washington for interceptors and for the deal with
Iran, which Washington signed in June without Israel's consent, and it is
therefore trying to move from aid to 'reciprocal partnership' before the MOU
expires in 2028 while the American public drifts away. In Europe the two logics
meet: Israel sells the continent weapons at record levels (EUR 3bn from Greece
alone) while governments sanction the settlements, and the friendly bloc (Czechia,
Slovakia, Slovenia, Austria) shields it only as long as it keeps winning
elections. Two signals that are not rows: the election of 27 October, in which
the main contenders for prime minister reject a Palestinian state, so that the policy survives a
change of prime minister, and the Lebanon talks, in which the state of Lebanon
signed a document that Hezbollah, the party that actually holds the weapons,
rejects. Israel's real question for 2027 is whether any of its partners will
carry the burden of the 'day after' that it declines to carry itself.

grand_strategy.reading: Italy is a middle power that lives by position rather than mass: a G7 and euro-area economy with a 137% debt, a security guarantee it does not pay for, and a coastline that makes Libya, Tunisia and the Hormuz strait domestic questions. Meloni's strategy, in Luttwak's terms, is to convert geography and access into rank - first on Trump, then on Brussels, then on Africa - while spending little force. It worked in 2025 (the first European at the White House, Mercosur and the Russian assets shaped in Rome, a thaw with Berlin and Paris) and strains in 2026, when Washington turned from courting her to attacking her and the Iran war made basing, energy and migration one problem. The structure beneath is stable: NATO and the EU are not negotiable, so rhetoric moves around them (the refusal of troops for Ukraine, conditional recognition of Palestine, the Israel freeze) but never out. The real test is financial: the 5% pledge, the deficit procedure and an energy bill set by third parties leave little room for the posture of 'bridge'.

grand_strategy.reading:
Jordan runs the grand strategy of a small, resource-poor monarchy whose
neighbours are bigger than its means and whose population is not the one its
state was built for. It has no leverage of its own, so it sells position: a
border no one else can hold, airspace over which wars are fought, a port, a
training ground, a seat for mediation, and a King who is received everywhere.
Everything is organised around one fear, that the Palestinian question be
settled on its territory - by annexation of the West Bank, by displacement
from Gaza, or by a security 'substitute' arrangement that makes the army the
jailer of the West Bank. That fear explains why a treaty partner of 32 years
is now treated as the main threat (no ambassadors since November 2023, the
energy-for-water swap refused, the annexation 'red line'), why the kingdom
still shoots down Iranian missiles over its own land, and why it will not
break with Tehran. The Luttwak pattern is that each safeguard enlarges the
exposure it was meant to cover: patrons make it a target, the ban on the
Brotherhood removes a valve, the aid corridor invites closure, the diplomatic
snub removes the leverage over the supplies that Israel can still cut. Two
signals that are not rows: the King travelled to Malaysia and Australia on
11 October 2026 while a Houthi strike on Riyadh airport killed a Jordanian,
so the King's presence abroad rather than at home is itself a choice; and
Israeli elections are due in October 2026, so the annexation threat will be
tested by the next coalition, not by this one.

grand_strategy.reading: Japan is the case of a power that rearmed by naming its contingency, and then met the coalition the naming provoked. Luttwak's logic of strategy says that what is declared is not what is deterred: Takaichi's sentence of 7 November 2025 turned a quiet ambiguity into a position, and a position can be answered. Beijing answered on every lever that Japan had left exposed (tourists, seafood, rare earths, dual-use exports), recruited Moscow in a single sentence about 'militarism', and then waited; eleven months later the retraction it demands has not come and neither has the thaw (Wang Yi to Iwaya, 28 September 2026). Tokyo's compensation is the oldest one in its strategy, the American alliance, now bought with USD 550bn and paid in installments, and a ring of lesser partnerships (Manila, Canberra, New Delhi, London and Rome, Seoul) that each add a little weight and none a guarantee. The constraint that matters is not Article 9, which the February 2026 landslide has put in play, but arithmetic: a shrinking population, a debt of 230% of GDP, a yen at 160, and a Strait of Hormuz that closed in March. The grand strategy therefore has the shape of a lever with a short arm: the deterrent is credible, the base that pays for it is not yet. The test of the next twelve months is whether the rewritten security documents (due by the end of 2026) and a possible Xi-Takaichi meeting at the APEC summit in Shenzhen (18-19 November) can turn the naming into a negotiated line before the bill comes due.

grand_strategy.reading:
Kazakhstan is the small-state manoeuvre between three great powers, played by a
state that is not small in size but is in leverage: its long northern border
and its pipelines belong to the neighbour it must not offend, its money
comes more and more from China and the West, and its security was lent to it by
Russia in January 2022. In Luttwak's terms Astana practises the weaker party's
relational manoeuvre: it never chooses, because each patron's offer is worth
more as long as the others are watching. The constraint that disciplines the
whole system is the 2022 debt, which is paid not in money but in language: an
'alliance' declaration (12 Nov 2025), a Russian reactor (28 May 2026), CSTO and
EAEU seats kept. Every clear no (the 'republics', the sanctions pledge, the
Kazakh language) is balanced by a visible yes. Since 2025 the structure has
thickened on all three sides at once, which is the best test of a hedge: Trump
received the five presidents and Kazakhstan joined the Abraham Accords and the
Board of Peace; Xi came to Astana and then received Tokayev in Shanghai
(16 Jul 2026); Putin returned the Moscow visit with a state visit to Astana
(27-29 May 2026). The weak point is not a patron but a place: the CPC terminal
at Novorossiysk, where Russian ownership, Western capital and Ukrainian drones
meet. Signals that are not rows: Lavrov did not attend the Moscow talks of
11-12 Nov 2025 (an unusual absence), and the Druzhba stoppage of Kazakh oil to
Germany reported for 1 May 2026 arrived while Rosatom's contract was being
finished. With the new constitution in force since 1 July 2026, the open question
is whether the system survives the man: a presidential succession in 2029 would
reopen the question of who owes what to whom.

grand_strategy.reading:
Kenya plays the strategy of a middle power without a hegemon's resources: it
has no oil, an exhausted treasury and a restless street, and what it can sell
is the room itself. It hosts the talks nobody else can host (South Sudan's
Tumaini track, the DRC process, even the founding charter of the Sudanese army's enemy), supplies
police and soldiers to missions that other states design (Haiti, AUSSOM),
shelters the UN's Nairobi offices, and takes money from everyone who wants a
voice in East Africa - China's yuan loans, Gulf fuel credit, Washington's
health compact, London's training ground, Brussels' preferences. Luttwak's
reading is that the position is rented, not owned: the broker is indispensable
only while the great powers need a neutral address, and each act that proves
indispensability - the RSF charter, Madobe's Jubaland, the Haiti command - is
the one that draws a retaliation (Sudan's import ban), a quarrel (Mogadishu)
or a bill (Haitian crowds, Gen Z at home). Domestically the clock is the 2027
election: the Odinga pact that carried Ruto's broad-based government died
with Raila on 15 October 2025, and every foreign choice is made with the
street and the debt service (interest about 45% of ordinary revenue) in view.
Signals that are not rows. First, a 'two pillars' formula attributed to Ruto
was not found in any source read; what the sources do record is
'a bridge between East and West' (Beijing, April 2025), which is a hedge
rather than a choice. Second, the US embassy in Nairobi lacked a confirmed
ambassador for a long stretch of 2026 although the December 2025 health
compact was signed in Washington: the American attention is real but thin.
Third, Kenya recognised Morocco's sovereignty over Western Sahara in April
2026 and Kosovo in March 2025: recognition looks like a currency Nairobi spends
where partners pay, an unsentimental turn from its old non-aligned posture
(our reading, not a sourced motive). The
open question is the Odinga succession: if ODM fractures, the foreign
portfolio loses its domestic anchor before the vote.

grand_strategy.reading:
South Korea is a middle power that has turned itself into something every
great power needs - memory chips, shipyards, reactors, howitzers - and has
then discovered that being needed is not the same as being secure. Luttwak's
reading is of an alliance that pays for its own guarantor: the 1953 treaty
and 28,500 soldiers remain the fact on which everything rests, but since
2025 the guarantor sets a price in tariffs, investment pledges, weapons
purchases and support payments, cuts the allied exercises on its own
initiative to court the adversary, and moves air-defence batteries to another
theatre. Seoul answers with the only strategic move open to a rich dependent:
make itself more useful (MASGA, the USD 350bn fund) and more autonomous
(nuclear submarines, enrichment, wartime control) at once, which are
contradictory signals to a guarantor. On the other front stands a deterrence
facing an adversary that has stopped talking: Pyongyang has replaced hostility
to be negotiated with a border to be built, with Russian money and combat
experience behind it, and Lee's outreach - loudspeakers off, regret for drones,
a proposal to end the war - meets a wall of mines and silence. The restoration
of ties with China and Japan in 2026 is the third leg: a hedge, not an
alignment, and the one that Beijing's own Wang Yi describes as 'strategic
autonomy'. Signals that do not fit a row: Putin's January 2026 wish to
'restore ties' and Seoul's ambassador at Vladivostok, while the Hyundai
option on its St Petersburg plant lapsed; and the disclosure of two North
Korean prisoners transferred from Ukraine, which turned Kyiv from a cause into
a quarrel in September-October 2026.

grand_strategy.reading:
Kuwait is a small rich state whose strategy has been, since 1961, to buy
protection with money and mediation and to keep every neighbour a little in debt
to it. 2024-2026 broke the model on two fronts at once. At home the Emir ended
the one thing that distinguished Kuwait in the Gulf, an elected assembly with
real vetoes: he governs by decree, passed the debt law that the Assembly had
blocked, and used the nationality law as a welfare and political instrument. Abroad
the 2026 war with Iran turned the host of the largest US ground presence in the
region into the Gulf state that is struck most often: the guarantor from 1991
could not stop Iranian drones, and the 'we allowed no use of our land' line is
as much a plea to Tehran as a statement of fact. The paradox that runs
through the card is that every protection Kuwait buys has a price in exposure:
the US bases invite attack, the Chinese-built port on Bubiyan invites Iraqi and
Iranian pressure, the decree rule that unlocked the money costs it the
institutions that absorb shocks, and the extra partners (Pakistan, India, the UK)
add cover, not guarantees. Two signals that are not rows: the Emir's description
of Iran as a 'friend' even while it attacks, which keeps a way back open, and the
absence of any Kuwaiti step toward Israel when its neighbours debate it.
Questions for the next pass: the outcome of Iraq's Federal Supreme Court on the
Khor Abdullah appeal (hearings were postponed to mid-June 2025), Kuwait's own
reaction to the June 2025 Israel-Iran war, the current status of the Durra
negotiations, and the Kuwait-China oil trade, which this pass could not source.

grand_strategy.reading: Lebanon's grand strategy since Aoun's election (9 January 2025) and Salam's government (February 2025) is the strategy of a state trying to become the owner of its own war and peace. The aim is simple to state: one army, one decision on war, Israel out, money in. The means are borrowed: American brokerage, Saudi and Qatari money, European training, Egyptian ideas, a UN mandate that is ending. The 2026 war showed the gap between the declared monopoly and the actual one: Hezbollah fired on 2 March in spite of the cabinet's own ban, and the state paid in dead, displaced and territory. Beirut's answer is not to fight Hezbollah (the army will not, and the state would not survive it) but to move the country's major patrons into a sequence in which Israeli withdrawal, army deployment and donor money arrive together. That is why it signed a framework with a state it does not recognise and why it avoids the word normalisation. It is a strategy of patience and bargaining from weakness, and its test is the pilot zones: if Israel does not withdraw from a place the army has actually cleared, the Shia community will keep its arms for good and the state's whole case will fall. Syria and the Gulf matter because they take the land and sea borders and the money out of Iran's hands; Russia, China and Turkey are marginal. This card is dated 12 October 2026, before the next round of Israel-Lebanon military talks planned for 20-21 October and the EU's formal decision on the army mission.

recognition.note: Two rival governments. This card is the internationally recognised Government of National Unity in Tripoli (prime minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah), listed by the United Nations as Libya's government. The House of Representatives voted on 13 Aug 2024 to end its term and backs a rival Government of National Stability in Benghazi (the Hammad government), whose military arm is Khalifa Haftar's Libyan National Army; Haftar's camp holds most of the oilfields. The eastern authority has no actor of its own in the atlas: it is recorded through this card's objectives, constraints and actions, and through the other cards that deal with it.

objectives.text: Remain the sole UN-recognised government, and in office, until an election on terms Dbeibah can survive. grand_strategy.reading: Libya is a state whose two halves are each a client, and the card of the recognised half has to be read as the card of a client that holds the title deeds. Tripoli has the United Nations list, a Turkish shield, the Central Bank and the Italian gas contract; Benghazi has the oilfields, the army, Russian air bases at six sites, the Emirati air bridge to Kufra and the Egyptian border. Luttwak's relational manoeuvre turns on seams between an opponent and its allies, and here the seams are in the patrons themselves: Turkey backs Tripoli and courts Haftar's son, Egypt trains the east's officers and sends its intelligence chief to Dbeibah, Italy and Greece pay both coasts, and Washington brokers a unified budget and a power-sharing scheme that would make Saddam Haftar president. Every patron has a reason to keep the division manageable and none to end it: a united Libya would answer to one capital, and each of them has a deal with a different one. The 2026 state is a stalemate that is eroding - a unified budget (11 Apr), a Tripoli agreement on an elections commission and a single executive (30 Aug), a House that endorsed it and a High Council that did not, UNSMIL's mandate up for renewal on 31 Oct, new fighting in Zawiya - and the paradox of the card is that Dbeibah's best moves (purging the militias, courting Washington, selling Europe departures) each work for the east as well or better, so Tripoli's strength is its recognition, which is the one asset the UN process is designed to retire.

grand_strategy.reading:
Sri Lanka is a small island on the Indian Ocean sea lanes, and its foreign policy is driven first by money: the IMF programme, creditors, Gulf remittances and fuel imports. The Dissanayake government (NPP, in office since September 2024) tries to turn that position into several deals at once. India gets energy, defence and the grid; China keeps Hambantota and the refinery it has already signed for; the EU and the US keep trade preference and tariff relief in play.
The line it calls neutral is a constraint as much as an instrument. It keeps every lender open, and it is what a debt setback, a fishermen's dispute, a Tamil vote in Geneva or a Gulf oil shock would test first.

grand_strategy.reading:
Lithuania is a small state that has chosen to be a front-line state on purpose:
it argues for the threat louder than anyone and buys the insurance before the
allies are asked to. The ranked objectives are a ladder from Russia, to the
allies' soldiers, to Ukraine, and the means mirror them - the most defence
spending in NATO relative to GDP, borrowed money from the EU to turn a brigade
into a division, and treaty exits that trade moral position for capability.
The Luttwakian friction appears wherever one rung undermines another. Border
closure and sanctions on Belarus defend the frontier but hand Minsk hostages;
leaving the mine and cluster conventions and lifting the nuclear ban deter
Moscow but enlarge Moscow's narrative; and the offer to pay for a permanent
US base binds the security of the state to a patron that is simultaneously
easing sanctions on Russian diesel and Belarusian potash. Domestic politics
adds noise, not direction: three Social Democratic cabinets in two years, a
president and a foreign minister who anchor the line on Russia, Ukraine and
Poland, and an open split on China. The Russia grade is adversary because the
Seimas calls its regime terrorist and the national assessments treat it as the
only state that can attack Lithuania; Belarus is a rival because Vilnius
aims at pressure and isolation, not at the end of the regime, and the line
softens when Washington pushes. The year to watch is 2027: the German brigade
complete, the nuclear amendment's final vote (planned 12 Jan 2027), the EU
sanctions renewal on potash, and a US rotation that may or may not become a base.

grand_strategy.reading:
Luxembourg runs the strategy of a rich small state that buys security with money and
with the right to host other people's institutions: the EU courts, the bank hubs, the
satellite company. Its 2% benchmark, its Ukraine pact and its EU votes are paid for by
a financial centre that depends on the Greater Region's commuters, and that centre is
also where the Russian assets are custodied. The drone closure of its single airport in
September 2026 is the first sign that a state so reliant on one hub and one airport has
no margin if it is attacked; the origin is unknown and the reading must stay open.

grand_strategy.reading:
Latvia is the textbook case of Luttwak's weak-state strategy: a country of 1.9
million with a long border and a large Russian-speaking population cannot win
an attritional contest with Russia, so it plays the paradoxical game of making
itself too costly to attack and too connected to be left alone. Every pillar
borrows weight from outside: the Canadian-led brigade and Article 5 for
deterrence, EU money and the escape clause for the budget, German and American
factories for the kit, Lithuania's terminal for the gas. The strategy is
consistent but its cost is dependence on partners whose own commitment is
wavering (US rotation gaps, weapons delays, the Pentagon posture review) and on
an internal politics that has shown it can fall to a single drone: the May 2026
crisis, the 52% turnout and 25% of the vote for two populist parties, one
openly pro-Russian, are the soft flank. Russia is graded adversary because the
Latvian state itself names it the existential threat and a sponsor of terrorism,
not because Riga seeks its regime's end; Belarus is a rival whose pressure is
cheap to apply and costly to stop. Two signals that are not rows: the
Silina government fell over an air-defence failure, not over foreign policy
(Kulbergs, who took over, promised to hold defence at 5% of GDP and keep a hard
line on Moscow), and part of the Russian-speaking population is still outside
the citizenry (non-citizens were 9% of residents in 2024), so the election
measures only part of the minority's weight.

grand_strategy.reading:
Morocco runs the strategy of a state that has turned a territorial claim into a currency and gets its partners to pay in it: the price of a warm relationship with Rabat
is a sentence on the autonomy plan, and between 2020 and 2026 Washington, Madrid, Paris, London, Brussels and Bamako paid it, with the Security Council text of 31 October 2025 as
the receipt. That is Luttwak's relational manoeuvre in its cleanest form. The side that is weaker in arms (USD 5.5bn against Algeria's 21.8bn) did not match the budget; it widened the circle
around the dispute until the rival's position became the minority one, and it spends on infrastructure that serves the claim (Dakhla, the highway, the pipeline) rather than on tanks.
The paradoxes show where the currency inflates. The migration valve that buys European votes set off the Ceuta crossing of July 2026 and a Spanish refusal to discuss sovereignty;
the Israeli bargain gave Algiers its encirclement story; integrating the territory widens every partner's legal exposure after the Court of Justice rulings of October 2024; and the showcase
politics of AFCON and 2030 sit beside a youth that took to the streets over hospitals and schools. Signals that are not rows: the US imposed a 12.5% tariff on Morocco on 24 July 2026,
three weeks after the king announced a highway to be named for Trump, so a patron's goodwill on the Sahara does not buy tariff relief; Algeria's absence from the Council vote is a refusal
to be bound, not a concession; and the next test is the MINURSO renewal due before 31 October 2026 and whether the framework agreement the US wanted before the summer ever takes shape.

grand_strategy.reading: Moldova is a state whose strategy is to turn its geography into a European fact before Russia turns it into a Russian one. PAS and Sandu hold three keys at once: a parliamentary majority renewed on 28 September 2025 despite a funded opposition, a candidate status that became real negotiations in June 2026, and a security web (EU, Romania, Ukraine, the US in Congress) that substitutes for the alliance that neutrality forbids. The central Luttwakian pattern is that every victory in the East is paid for on the Transnistrian and Gagauz flanks: cutting Gazprom and Cuciurgan freed the right bank from blackmail but ruined the left bank it hopes to reintegrate; defending elections with courts and bans hardens the audience Moscow has always had in Comrat; and tying accession to Ukraine's carries both momentum and the Hungarian veto. Two signals that are not rows: the decision to recall the ambassador from Moscow rather than expel the Russian embassy, which keeps the channel that Russia's own embassy says it wants; and Sandu's June 2026 call to put the Russian withdrawal into any Ukraine settlement, which her own foreign minister resists. Whether Moscow is an adversary is a question the ontology answers by structure: Russia's declared aim in Chișinău is a compliant government, not the end of Moldova, and Moldova's aim is a Russian departure, not Russian defeat, so the grade is rival, the hardest rival on the map.

grand_strategy.reading:
Mexico is a state that cooperates with its strongest neighbour in order to keep that neighbour out of its territory, and Sheinbaum, in office since October 2024, has held that line with a steady sovereignty language. Its posture toward the United States is reluctant partnership: it hands over cartel figures, accepts CIA flights and the National Guard at the border, and refuses troops and unilateral strikes, while the USMCA stays unrenewed and the tariff exemption is the lever of the 2026 review. Mexico hedges through the EU agreement and tariffs on Chinese goods rather than through alignment with anyone, so its foreign policy is measured less by the partners it picks than by how far Washington lets it pick. Its weakest flanks are at home: a judicial reform that frightens investors, a Pemex still losing money on about USD 80bn of debt, and a remittance flow that deportations and the 1% tax are already shrinking.

Added 2026-10-16 (protagonist pass). The tariff picture has changed since the first draft: the Supreme Court ended the fentanyl tariffs on 20 February 2026 and what Washington now holds is the Section 301 duty on non-USMCA goods, the Section 232 sectoral duties and, above all, the annual review of the agreement, which is the real lever; the talks were reported stalled on 12 October with Trump asking for energy deals. The cartels work for Washington as a pretext (terrorist designations, the claim of links to the government) and for Mexico as a bargaining chip (92 transferred, El Mencho killed) at once, and the same ambivalence marks the region: Mexico shouts non-intervention over Venezuela and Peru and says little where Washington's interests bite. Its second ring is thin but real: the EU agreement, a trade deficit with China it cannot cut without hurting its own exporters, and a Latin America in which Argentina is hostile, Colombia turns cooler after the change of government in Bogota, Chile is divided from Mexico over Bachelet, and only Brazil and, since August, Peru are back in regular contact.

grand_strategy.reading: Under President Hilda Heine, the Marshall Islands runs its foreign policy inside a treaty it cannot leave cheaply: the Compact pays for the state and carries its defence, and the 2023 extension bought twenty years, not a settlement of the nuclear grievance. Inside that frame it has three instruments it actually uses: the Taipei tie, one of three Pacific recognitions left; a flag registry, second largest in the world as of 2017, whose foreign-owned ships the United States said it would not defend at sea; and the visa-free right to live and work in America, which makes emigration a lever. The sea is the one constraint no treaty can renegotiate: the country averages seven feet above sea level, and a US$1 billion radar site at Kwajalein is on the list of what rising seas could threaten.

grand_strategy.reading:
North Macedonia runs the strategy of a state that has already paid for entry
twice and now treats a third payment as a trap. It changed its name for NATO
(2018-20), accepted the French proposal for the EU (2022), and still has no date;
the Mickoski government, in office since June 2024 after winning 58 of 120 seats, draws the
conclusion that every concession reopens the account, and trades speed for
guarantees. The result is the Luttwakian pattern of a weak actor playing a long
game against two veto-holders: it keeps the one thing it has already won (NATO,
near-total alignment with Brussels on Russia and Ukraine) and widens its list of
patrons, with Washington, Ankara and, until Orban's fall, Budapest and Belgrade
behind it. The price is a country neither inside nor outside the EU, and a
population that votes with its feet. Two signals that are not rows: the
Commission's report of November 2025 states flatly that 'no attempts were made' to
adopt the amendments, while von der Leyen's visit of 2 October 2026 produced the
first agreed step in years, so the next weeks (the foreign minister's trip to Sofia
during a Corridor 8 event) are the test of whether the 'stronger pressure' Mickoski
awaits has arrived. Open gaps: no source was found on Russian influence on the
2024 vote, on Chinese projects under this government, or on any Greek retaliation
after 2024.

grand_strategy.reading: Mali plays the strategy of a junta that has swapped its old friends for new patrons: it expelled France and left ECOWAS, took Russian soldiers and drones, and bet its revenue on gold that the state now runs itself. The bet holds at the centre and fails at the edges, where the Africa Corps has left Kidal, the JNIM blockade chokes the Dakar and Abidjan corridors, and the Azawad front takes the north. Sovereignty is the regime's only proof of legitimacy, so every concession to a neighbour or to Algeria reads at home as a loss, and that is why the rift with Algiers lasted a year. Watch whether Moscow and Ankara keep paying for the north when the gold and the corridor no longer cover the cost.

grand_strategy.reading: Myanmar's strategy is that of a client whose army lives on its usefulness to others. After 2021 the Tatmadaw lost the periphery but kept the centre, the air force and what its patrons want: a government in Naypyidaw that signs the Kyaukphyu port and the pipelines for Beijing, the Kaladan corridor for Delhi, the nuclear and refinery contracts for Moscow, and a border that stays quiet for Bangkok. Luttwak's logic runs through the patron's calculus: China does not need the junta to win, it needs the border calm, the pipelines open, the scam business under control and no Western-aligned government in Naypyidaw, so it brokers just enough ceasefires (Lashio, pressure on the TNLA) to keep the army alive and no more, while the KIA, the UWSA and others keep the leverage that lets Beijing bargain with both sides. The 2025-26 election and the presidency convert that client status into an appearance of normality: the four governments that already dealt with the regime (China, Russia, India, Thailand) now deal with a president, while ASEAN as a body and the West have only renewed their pressure. Each concession that buys survival, from Lashio to Kyaukphyu to the rare-earth promises, gives some other power a veto over the army's next move. Rakhine is the test: the Arakan Army, not Naypyidaw, now decides whether Kyaukphyu, Sittwe and the Bangladesh border, which are three patrons' interests at once, are safe.

grand_strategy.reading: Montenegro runs the grand strategy of a twenty-year-old micro-state that has bet its survival on being absorbed into the institutions that guarantee small states: NATO (done in 2017) and the EU (the 2028 target). The method is alignment as proof - full CFSP alignment, expulsions of Russian operatives, a defence budget above 2% - and the resource is speed: it is the only candidate with 18 chapters closed. The Luttwakian trap is that the last chapters are not technical. Croatia's veto turns on wartime grievances from the 1990s, and the Spajic majority rests on parties that treat the 2006 independence as a wound, so every step that pleases Belgrade's friends at home (the Jasenovac resolution, the Mladic condolences) costs a vote in Zagreb or The Hague, while every step toward Brussels costs the coalition's Serbian flank. The same logic runs through the economy: the Gulf and Turkish capital that replaces Chinese debt arrives with procedure-bypassing laws that the Commission itself flags. Two signals that are not rows: the cadence of closures (December 2025, January, March, June and July 2026) and President Milatovic's repeated returns of laws to Parliament, a veto that keeps the Constitutional Court and Brussels in the loop. With the Serbian election on 25 Oct 2026 and Montenegro's own on June 2027, the question is whether the accession treaty can be finished before the identity politics of one of the two neighbours changes the arithmetic.

objectives.text: Stay sovereign between two giants by spreading ties to third neighbours. The phrase is current: in Washington on 2 Aug 2023 PM Oyun-Erdene called the United States an 'important strategic third neighbor' and said that a landlocked Mongolia would suffer if great-power rivalry turned into a new Cold War. grand_strategy.reading:
Mongolia runs a strategy of buffering: a landlocked state between Russia and China
that sells its ground (coal, copper, gold) to one neighbour, buys its fuel from the other,
and calls the spread of other partners a third neighbour policy. The posture is neutral
in words and dependent in structure. The 2024 election gave the Mongolian People's Party
68 of 126 seats, a narrow majority after a supermajority, and the 2025 shift at the top
came from the street and from the house: Prime Minister Oyun-Erdene lost a confidence vote
on 3 June 2025 with 44 votes against the 64 needed, and parliament confirmed Zandanshatar
on 13 June. Later accounts disagree: Al Jazeera reports Zandanshatar losing a confidence
vote and resigning in October 2025, while Wikipedia's crisis summary says a presidential veto
and a court ruling kept him in office; a 2026 cabinet infobox records a dissolution in April
2026 with a successor. Current leadership is not confirmed here. The two dated acts that show
the strategy at work are the Putin visit of September 2024 (the ICC warrant unenforced
under fuel dependence) and the September 2025 PoS-2 memorandum (the transit fee as a bet, the
price still open). A non-event is a signal: Mongolia is not an observer of the Organization of
Turkic States (OTS observers page), although the OTS secretary-general visited Ulaanbaatar in
March 2025 at the Mongolian foreign minister's invitation. Gaps not closed here: the Mongolian
script question in detail, the Turkish and Kazakh bilateral figures, the India refinery (1.5 Mt,
Indian investment, construction pushed to 2028 per one commentary, tier 4), the EU beyond the
2017 agreement, and any US contact after 2023.

grand_strategy.reading: Mauritius wants the Chagos back and has the 2025 treaty as its best instrument, but ratification now waits on a US consent that Washington withholds and that London has accepted it cannot secure for now. Meanwhile Port Louis plays the two Asian powers against each other for money and security, India through funding and an enhanced partnership, China through a loan and a free trade agreement, without an alliance with either. grand_strategy.reading: Malawi's grand strategy in 2026 is to keep the currency and the budget alive while its donors leave: the IMF programme lapsed in May 2025 and no successor was agreed by August 2026, and the UK and the US have cut or withdrawn money. Its external ties are transactional (the US through a visa channel that is narrowing, Tanzania over the lake, where the prize is oil and gas) and the lake dispute is the one territorial stake the card can read. grand_strategy.reading:
Malaysia is the middle power that chairs the room and sells neutrality in it. Its currency is access, not force: Xi in April 2025 and Trump in October, Hamas's political wing and Washington's trade negotiators, BRICS partner status and the Five Power Defence Arrangements, all at once. In Luttwak's terms its strength is that the other powers cannot settle the room without it, and its weakness is that the neutrality has to be re-earned each time a power presses. The 2025 chair is the clearest case: the Putrajaya ceasefire and the Kuala Lumpur accord gave Kuala Lumpur a stage, then Thailand's suspension and the December fighting showed that the stage rested on Trump's attention; the reciprocal trade deal repeated the pattern in 2026, signed in October, voided in March, yet still setting the tariff. At home the logic runs the other way: the Malay vote that rewards Gaza and neutrality is the one UMNO, PAS and Najib's pardon now contest, and the election is due within 16 months.
Signals that are not rows: Anwar in Shanghai in September 2026 saying that Malaysia stays neutral and that Beijing understood; UMNO's dare of the same month; the rail extension to the Thai border agreed in principle and not yet approved. Gaps in this pass (no source read, nothing written): Japan, Turkey (drones, the Islamic axis), Saudi Arabia and the Gulf (hajj, petrochemicals), Iran (ship-to-ship transfers), and the detail of Australia, the UK and New Zealand beyond the FPDA; Singapore's water price and Pedra Branca rest on one tier-4 pointer.

grand_strategy.reading: Niger's junta has traded the old French security partnership for a Russian guard and a regional bloc of juntas, and it has tried to pay for its isolation by taking the uranium and the oil out of foreign hands. Its two real problems are geography and war: a landlocked state whose only outlets run through Benin and the Nigerian frontier, and a Tillabéri border where JNIM and the Islamic State's Sahel province strike the bases and the capital's airport. The paradox is that each act of sealing the state off, from the Benin border to the ECOWAS exit to the expulsions, shrinks the outlets the uranium and the oil need, while the Russian guard protects the capital and not the provinces where the state is losing. Luttwak's reading is a regime that chose isolation as a defence and must now buy its way back out through partners it has already expelled.

grand_strategy.reading: Nigeria is the region's indispensable state and a leader short of the means to lead: it holds the oil, the population and the ECOWAS flag, but its money goes to debt service, its north is pressed from the Sahel, and it relies on outside force and outside capital to fight insurgents it cannot beat alone. Its moves work against its aims in three places: the Sahel, where the ECOWAS sanctions on Niger drove the AES out and left the Lake Chad force without Niger; the oil, where the refinery built to end imports takes the crude that earns the dollars; and Paris and Washington, where the partners it courts bring frictions it must then manage at home. The 2027 election will decide whether the reform record survives its costs, which makes every concession to a partner a domestic question. Enriched on 2026-10-16: the patron it leans on is also the one that labels it (CPC, Child Soldiers Act listing), the giant could not fly a transport home through Burkina's sky without an apology, and the strong naira is a reform success whose benefit to the budget is unproven; Abuja's answer is to spread its bets (Ankara, the Gulf, Brasilia, Delhi, BRICS) rather than to pick a patron. This is a structural reading built on thin evidence (most rows are C, and the gaps are listed in the stance notes), not a verdict on Abuja's intentions.

grand_strategy.reading:
The Netherlands runs the grand strategy of a trading state that has no army large
enough to protect its trade and has therefore chosen to be useful to everyone who
does: the United States as guarantor, Germany as the other half of its land
forces, Belgium as the other half of its navy, Britain for amphibious power, and
Ukraine as the place where its air force, drones and legal arguments are tested.
The cabinet's own formula - a European pillar inside NATO - is the Luttwakian
answer of a small power: raise the cost of leaving it alone, never the cost of
defending it. What changed in 2025-26 is that the guarantor itself became a source
of friction (Greenland tariffs, the Venezuela operation, the Iran war, export
controls on ASML) and a second, equally important customer - China - showed with
Nexperia how much leverage it holds over Dutch and European industry. The new
government answers with money (3.5%), a softer line toward Beijing and a harder
one toward Israel, but it governs with 66 seats. Signals that are not rows: the
October 2025 tie between D66 and the PVV (Wilders is in opposition, the second
largest party), the Dutch foreign minister's March 2026 phone call with Wang Yi, the first
since the Nexperia row, and the defence minister's admission that Dutch aid to
Ukraine has reached a ceiling. Open question: whether a minority cabinet can fund
the rearmament without losing the 2025 coalition's consensus on Ukraine.

grand_strategy.reading: Norway runs the strategy of a rich small state on the edge of a hostile great power: its security is borrowed from the Atlantic alliance, its wealth comes from the thing Europe needs most, and both are now wielded under pressure. Since 2022 it has turned its income into the three things it can use: gas for Europe's grid, the Nansen programme for Ukraine, and a defence budget heading for 3.5% of GDP. The classic Luttwakian pattern is that each lever works against the next: gas and the fund make Norway central and rich, but also a target and, for Washington, an object to press (tariffs, the fund's ethics, the Greenland episode). In response it is pluralising its guarantors (UK frigates and Lunna House, German submarines, the EU defence partnership, Nordic integration with Sweden and Finland), while remaining dependent on US aircraft and US reinforcement. With Russia the policy is firm and unromantic: sanctions, public naming of GPS jamming and espionage, but also a fisheries regime and a Svalbard Treaty that Oslo wants to keep working. The seizure of the Professor Molchanov on 2 Sep 2026 shows the limits of that dual policy; it will be tested next by the Russian appeal and by how far Moscow pushes Svalbard. Domestically the Støre minority government depends on left parties whose priorities (oil phase-out, divestment from Israel) cut across the fund and the energy exports that give Norway its influence; the 2027 budget will test it again. Two signals that are not rows: Norway refused a seat on the Board of Peace on principle, and its Arctic Council chairship ended in May 2025 with Russia still excluded from political dialogue, so the forum Norway invested in is now under Danish-Greenlandic stewardship in the middle of the Greenland dispute. Gaps: the rate of the US tariff now in force, the US Marine rotation (only prepositioning and exercises are sourced), the 2024-25 restrictions on Chinese investment (no source found; only Security Act screening, the Telenor-Huawei decision of 2019 and the 2026 threat assessments are documented), and the US share of the fund's equity.

grand_strategy.reading: Nepal is a landlocked hedger between India and China, and its grand strategy has been to get paid for its water and its people while keeping its border claims alive. The September 2025 Gen Z uprising, which brought down Oli and put Sushila Karki in charge of a six-month interim, ended with the March 2026 election, won outright by the Rastriya Swatantra Party (182 of 275 seats) and its prime minister Balendra Shah. The new government has to show that the India-China balance survives its own warmer reset with Delhi and the Lipulekh friction, and that the power and labour economy can carry the state through the next earthquake or flood.

grand_strategy.reading: Nauru has a small economy, and its budget and its migration business come from Canberra; its one lever outside Australia is the seabed sponsorship, which waits on rules the International Seabed Authority has not written. grand_strategy.reading: Hamas is a movement that lost the war it started and is trying to win the settlement. On the Luttwak reading, 7 Oct 2023 was an attack that destroyed its attacker's base and still redrew the map: Gaza is ruins, the military command was decapitated repeatedly (Deif, Yahya Sinwar, then his brother), Hezbollah and Iran were crippled, yet the Palestinian question is back on the table, recognitions of Palestine multiplied in 2025 and a US president personally owns a plan for Gaza. The cost of that outcome falls on Hamas, because every route to the state it helped bring back runs through its exclusion and its disarmament. Its strategy in 2026 is therefore delay with concessions on form: it gives up the hostages (the last bargaining chip, spent between 13 Oct 2025 and early 2026), dissolves its administration, accepts a technocratic committee and says yes to the 15-point roadmap, but holds the weapons and the tunnels as insurance, and tests whether the Board of Peace can force Israel to leave the Yellow Line first. Israel reads the same facts the other way (no withdrawal until disarmament), so the ceasefire exists on paper and bleeds on the ground: Hamas has not disarmed, Israel holds about 60% of the Strip, no stabilisation force and no technocratic committee has entered, and Israeli strikes on commanders have escalated since Sep 2026 ahead of Israel's 27 Oct election. Underneath sits a leadership choice made in July 2026: Hayya, the negotiator close to Iran, over Meshal, the Qatar-leaning pragmatist. The patrons are weaker or squeezed (Iran at war, Qatar bombed and pressed, Turkey vetoed from the force, Egypt hostile to Brotherhood rule), and the rival Palestinian Authority has just postponed the elections that might have given Hamas a legitimate way back. One signal that is not a row: Hamas announced a pause in public executions on 21 Oct 2025, days after Trump threatened to 'go in and kill them', so the order it keeps is partly a function of Washington's attention.

grand_strategy.reading: Hezbollah in October 2026 is a movement that has lost the war it was built to deter and has not yet lost the argument that justifies its weapons. Luttwak's logic shows twice. First, deterrence is a paradoxical good: an arsenal big enough to frighten Israel was also big enough to make destroying it Israel's priority, and the 'support front' of October 2023 handed Jerusalem the moment. Second, relational manoeuvre - the hidden, dispersed, community-embedded network, tied to Iran by a land bridge - beat Israeli firepower for eighteen years until Israeli intelligence penetrated the network itself: the pagers of 17 September 2024 and the decapitation that followed were less a military victory than the demonstration that the network had been read. Since then its position is that of a besieged political party with an army: the land route through Syria is shut by a hostile neighbour, Iranian cash comes by courier, the Lebanese state has banned its military activity and signed a framework that trades Israeli withdrawal for its disarmament, and its constituency is displaced and occupied. What keeps it from collapse is not strength but structure: a confessional system that cannot decide against the Shia community, an army that will not fight it, Amal as a brake on the state, and an Israeli occupation that supplies the justification. The open question for the next stage is whether the Lebanese state, with Gulf, US and European money behind its army, can turn the pilot zones into a precedent without provoking the clash both sides say they want to avoid, or whether Israel's tunnels-and-demolition campaign forces Hezbollah to choose between its arms and its place in the state.

grand_strategy.reading:
The Houthis are the clearest case in the atlas of a small actor that turned a
distant war into leverage over world shipping, and 2026 is the year in which
that leverage reached its culminating point. The Gaza war gave them a
justification, an audience and a free hand against the one trade route that
ties Asia to Europe; the 2025 US and Israeli campaigns cost them ports,
ministers and a chief of staff but not the capacity to hurt; the Iran war and
the closing of Hormuz then made Bab al-Mandab the only maritime outlet of the
Gulf, and on 3-11 September 2026 they took the whole Yemeni coast and Mayyun
to sit on it. In Luttwak's terms the movement has gone past the point where
each further success buys proportionally more: it has stretched its lines
into districts it cannot hold with consent, turned the Saudi restraint of
2022-25 into a Saudi-run coalition, and made the Kingdom an enemy it cannot
pay off, while the patron whose war created the opening is negotiating with
Washington. What it can still do is keep the threat of closure alive and
sell its absence, which is precisely what it did between the Gaza ceasefire
and July 2026 and what it needs to restore. Signals that are not rows: Iran's
foreign minister said in March that Tehran did not need its allies to join
its self-defence, the Houthis stayed out of the June 2025 war and waited four
weeks in 2026 before firing on Israel, and the Houthi leadership told China
and Russia their ships were not targets. All of it shows an actor that
chooses its wars; the open question for the autumn of 2026 is whether it
still can.

grand_strategy.reading:
The RSF is a militia that has tried to become a state: it took Darfur and the gold fields, and it declared its own government in 2025, but it has no recognition, its supply runs through the neighbours of Sudan, and the El Fasher record has made the genocide finding the frame of any settlement.
On the Luttwak reading its central paradox is that the patron that makes it strong, the UAE, is also the reason it cannot be recognised, and the army's retaking of Kordofan since January 2026 shows that a massacre can take territory without making a state.
Its truces are tactical pauses, not a change of aim, so the state in Khartoum remains the objective and the war continues.

grand_strategy.reading:
The SDF is a case study of a client whose usefulness to a patron was its entire
security. Built by the United States in 2015 as the ground force against ISIS, it
held a quarter of Syria and an oil-and-prison economy without the attributes of a
state: no recognition, no port, no friendly border, an Arab-majority hinterland held
by consent. Luttwak's rule - a patron's help lasts as long as the client serves the
patron's strategy, not its own - played out in three steps: Turkey and the SNA tested
it in December 2024 (Manbij lost, Tishrin and Kobani held with US mediation); the new
Damascus offered integration in March 2025 and the SDF stalled for decentralisation;
and when Syria joined the anti-ISIS coalition in November 2025 the counter-ISIS role
that justified the SDF was duplicated and then disowned. The January 2026 offensive
met no external opposition: the US called for a halt, brokered the terms and, within
three months, left. What remains is a negotiated afterlife: the force dissolved on
25 Aug 2026, its commander is a presidential adviser, Kurdish units survive as
brigades and local security, and the contest has moved from the battlefield to the
constitution. Signals that are not rows: the YPJ is still outside the army, and the
Kobani prison riot of 12 Sep 2026 shows the security vacuum in the Kurdish towns. The
grades in this card are those of an actor that no longer controls territory; read
them as a legacy card with live consequences.

grand_strategy.reading: New Zealand is a small, trade-dependent state whose security has rested on Australia and, at arm's length since the 1986 rift, on the United States, the nuclear-free law being the price it chose to pay. Its real frontier is the Pacific: the Cook Islands' partnership with China and the Chinese naval live-fire drill in the Tasman Sea in February 2025 show where its strategy is tested, and it answers with money, a defence build-up toward 2% of GDP and a closer defence relationship with Australia. Its commitments further afield (Ukraine training, Russia sanctions, the Philippines visiting-forces pact, the India trade deal) are real but modest, and on Palestine it held back recognition in September 2025.

grand_strategy.reading:
Oman in October 2026 is a neutral whose neutrality has been put under live fire.
Its whole strategy since Qaboos is to be useful to every side and enemy to none:
a venue for the Americans and the Iranians, a door to the Houthis, a berth for
the US, British and Indian navies, an oil seller to China, a land bridge for
the Gulf. The Iran war of 28 February 2026 tested each of those at once. Iranian
drones hit three Omani ports while Muscat was still hosting the talks, Trump
threatened twice to bomb the mediator, and the Hormuz deal Oman helped write
on 17 June was read by Tehran and Washington as two opposite things. Luttwak's
logic shows in that gap: the instruments of a small state's security (access,
mediation, a share of the Strait) are the same instruments that make it a
target and a suspect. What holds is that all sides still need Oman more than
they distrust it: the US needs a channel on Hormuz and the Houthis, Iran needs
the one Arab neighbour that answers its calls, the Saudis and Emiratis need a
southern flank that does not break. Signals that are not rows: the government
never answered Trump in public; Sultan Haitham flew to Abu Dhabi on 17 Aug,
the day of Trump's second threat, and to London on 2 July; the fiscal tax
reform of 2028 shows the leadership expects the oil rent to shrink. Open gaps in
this pass: Egypt, Jordan, Iraq, Pakistan, France and Russia (no sourced
reading yet), the exact terms of the Saudi road link, and a primary text for
the 2023 anti-normalisation measure.

grand_strategy.reading: The Union acts as a grand strategist only by accident. It has no army, no single voice and no budget that anyone loves; what it has is a market, a rulebook, a currency and the right to say yes or no to its neighbours. Read through Luttwak, that is a strategy of the second level: it exports order by attraction (enlargement, association, Growth Plan money, visa-free travel) and by exclusion (sanctions, frozen assets, trade defence), and it moves only when 27 governments consent. In 2026 the logic of consent has hardened into a posture: Russia is the declared threat, the United States has become a 'necessary partner' that cannot be left and cannot be trusted, China is a rival managed through quotas and licences, and the neighbourhood is a queue. The paradoxes all come from the same root - the Union is strongest where its rules are least contested and most exposed where it needs speed. It has just shown it can finance a war (EUR 90bn), outlast a spoiler (Orban's defeat on 12 Apr 2026) and ban a fuel (Russian gas), and it still cannot appoint an envoy, use the assets it froze or guarantee its own borders without Washington. The reading for the next year is whether the Ankara-era bargain - a more European NATO, a Union that pays - turns into capacity, or whether the 2028-34 budget, the Turnberry steel clause and the Hungarian reversal are only a pause.

grand_strategy.reading:
NATO is a strategy only in the sense that a coalition can have one: it does what
thirty-two governments can sign, and the signature is the product. Since 2022 its
Luttwakian logic has been straightforward at the top level (deter Russia, with
Article 5 as the whole point) and perverse in the levels that carry it. To keep the
one member that matters it has to make that member's complaint its own agenda -
more European money, more European forces, 'NATO 3.0' - and each concession
advertises how much of the deterrent was always American. The Ankara summit of
7-8 July 2026 settled the immediate question (Article 5 'ironclad', Russia the
long-term threat, EUR 70bn for Ukraine, over USD 50bn of procurements) in six
paragraphs, and left the structural ones open: Washington's posture review is due
to reach Hegseth on 6 November, Ukraine's door is neither shut nor opened, Spain
and Slovakia are outside the 5% logic, and the next summit, promised for Albania
by Rutte, has no date. Two signals that are not rows: the omission of China and of
any Ukraine-membership language from both declarations, and Rutte's repeated use of
the 'division of labour' with the EU as the way to make Europeans pay without calling
it a retreat. Read through Luttwak, the alliance's strength (the Article 5 promise
that everyone believes in enough to pay for) is also its weakness: the promise is
only as strong as the doubts of the one guarantor, so the alliance spends its
political capital managing the guarantor rather than the adversary.

grand_strategy.reading:
Pakistan plays the oldest game of the weaker state beside a stronger neighbour
and plays it harder than anyone: it does not try to match India, it tries to
make India's every move expensive by multiplying the relationships that stand
behind it. In Luttwak's terms this is relational manoeuvre, not attrition. China
supplies the hardware, Saudi Arabia and Turkey the pacts and the money, the
United States the late-arriving cover, and the nuclear deterrent the floor under
all of it. Since May 2025 the manoeuvre has paid unusually well: a field marshal
sits at the head of the armed forces, Washington and Tehran both use his
channel, and a treaty with Riyadh turned a decades-old Saudi-Pakistani tie of manpower
for money into a defence guarantee. The paradoxes come from the same source. The army's
political control is its own great strategic liability: it gives the state one
decisive voice for a crisis, but it ties the access to Western money, the EU
market and the IMF to the standing of one man and one institution, and it keeps
the civilian economy it must lean on in permanent emergency. The second
paradox is geographic: the victory of May 2025 was real in the air, but India
answered with the river, and a weaker state has no good reply to a lever it
cannot touch. Third, the western front turned the old strategy upside down: the
Taliban it once nursed as depth are now its most dangerous neighbour, and each
blow it lands in Kabul makes the TTP's sanctuary safer. Pakistan's four patrons
are also four creditors of influence, and the Saudi-Turkish pact, signed while
it brokers peace for Iran, is the first sign that they can be played against
each other as easily as it plays them. The thing to watch is not the next
crisis with India but whether the three constraints (the budget, the
Afghan border, the water) tighten at the same time while one man holds every
lever.

grand_strategy.reading:
The Philippines is a small naval power in a contest it cannot win by force and has
chosen not to fight by force. Its answer is two instruments of the weak: exposure
as the weapon (every Chinese act is filmed, dated and protested, so the grey zone
that Beijing chose in order to stay below the level of war becomes a legal and
reputational ledger) and alliance as the shield (a treaty of 1951 read to cover
coast-guard ships, nine sites, missile batteries, and since 2025 a ring of
visiting-forces agreements that makes the shield plural). Luttwak's logic shows
in the price of each. Transparency cannot be switched off for a compromise, so the
2024 understanding at Second Thomas Shoal is disowned at home even as it holds;
and the shield turns the archipelago into a forward base whose missiles, Marcos
admits, would pull the country into a Taiwan war. The alliance is also a bet on
two presidents: Washington's (a 2025 strategy that forgot Manila, a tariff moved
to 12.5% over forced labour) and Manila's own, because the foreign policy
depends on a government whose trust rating is 28-34% against a vice president
at 57-58% whose family prefers accommodation with Beijing. Hence China is graded
rival, not adversary: no side seeks the other's end, Lazaro protests and talks in
the same week, and 28.6% of imports still come from China. Signals that are not
rows: the Philippines' own defence secretary denying an understanding the foreign
ministry announced; and a Code of Conduct that Manila chairs toward and doubts.

grand_strategy.reading: Palau holds three cards out of proportion to its size: a Taipei recognition that Beijing wants, a US Compact and military access that Washington needs in the western Pacific, and the Forum meeting it hosted in 2026. Its money comes from Washington under the Compact and from tourists, a large share of them Chinese, so the government that refuses Beijing's price depends on Beijing's visitors. The paradox sits at the centre of the card: the cards that keep Palau's standing with Washington and Taipei are the ones that expose its economy to Beijing's pressure.

grand_strategy.reading: Poland is a frontline state that has turned geography into rank: it spends the most in NATO, hosts about 10,000 US troops and the logistics hub of the Ukraine war, and treats Russia not as a rival but as the standing threat. Its grand strategy is a double reinsurance. The Atlantic leg (American troops, F-35s, Patriot, hopes of a permanent base and of nuclear sharing) is run mostly by President Nawrocki; the European leg (SAFE money, the German pact, French deterrence talks, a revived Visegrad) is run by Tusk's government. They are complementary on paper and rivalrous in practice, and the Luttwak logic bites exactly there: the more Warsaw tries to be everyone's indispensable ally, the more each guarantor discounts a promise that two offices make differently. The same logic runs through its neighbours. Poland needs Ukraine standing but taxes it with grain bans and Volhynia; it needs Germany but keeps a reparations claim; it seals the Belarus border and in doing so cuts the Chinese rail traffic that crosses it. The grade of Russia is 'adversary' rather than 'rival' because Warsaw's own officials call Russian sabotage state terrorism and Russia the main threat to Poland and Central Europe, and because the Kremlin itself says relations have 'deteriorated completely'; against that, Poland has no aim of regime change in Russia, which is why the grade carries confidence B and not A. Ukraine is a 'reluctant ally' - indispensable, aligned by necessity, with an open historical wound - and Belarus a 'rival' that is warming only because Washington brokered a prisoner swap. The central uncertainty is what Poland is in 2027: a country whose security depends on a US president's mood, or one that has bought, built and borrowed enough to depend on itself.

grand_strategy.reading:
North Korea is Luttwak's small adversary that became useful to a great power and
sold its usefulness dear. For thirty years its strategy was survival by
nuisance: weapons as the one asset a poor, sanctioned state could produce. The
war in Ukraine gave that asset a buyer. Since the treaty of June 2024 Kim has
turned shells, missiles, labour and an expeditionary force into cash, fuel,
food and technology, escaped the diplomatic quarantine, and made both Moscow
and Beijing court him. He has also removed the questions that used to bind
him: the UN panel is gone, denuclearisation is struck from every agenda,
reunification is struck from the constitution, and the Party Congress of
February 2026 wrote the status into policy. Pyongyang no longer asks to be
admitted to the order; it asks that the arsenal be accepted as a fact. The
paradoxes are all of one kind. Each success rests on a patron's need, not on
a strength of Pyongyang's own: the Russian income ends with the war, the
Chinese trade ends when Beijing chooses, the nuclear status leaves nothing to
bargain with, and the sanctions workaround turns the cyber and labour
earners into the targets of a coalition that no veto can dissolve. Two
signals that are not rows: the Ninth Congress's work report did not mention
Russia or China, and Kim has not met a US president since 2019 while Trump
keeps saying he will. The open question for 2027 is whether the same hand can
manage the end of the Russian war, a Trump offer that asks for the arsenal,
and a thirteen-year-old heir.

grand_strategy.reading:
Portugal runs the strategy of a small Atlantic state that makes itself useful to
every large power around it and commits to none beyond what the treaties force.
Its anchors are three - the EU (money and a Portuguese chair of the European
Council), NATO and the United States (Lajes), and the Lusophone world (Brazil,
Angola, the CPLP) - and its method is conditionality: base access on conditions,
Palestine recognised only with a group, the F-35 kept open, Chinese capital welcomed
but not endorsed. This works while the anchors do not collide. In 2026 they began to:
the Iran war put Lajes between Washington and the Spanish line, the F-16 replacement
asks it to choose between Lockheed and a European hedge it cannot yet pay for, and
the CPLP is splitting over Equatorial Guinea. At home the cost shows in a minority
government, a president of the other party who speaks more sharply than the foreign
minister, and Chega, which polls first on the one issue (immigration) where the
Lusophone strategy and the electorate pull apart. Expect Lisbon to stay the quietest
reliable ally until Washington asks for something it cannot dress in conditions.

grand_strategy.reading:
The State of Palestine is a state whose government cannot protect its people, finance itself or even hold an election, and it knows it: its grand strategy is the strategy of staying in
the picture. Everything Ramallah does is a bet that the Palestinian question will be settled by others and that whoever is still standing, with a flag, a seat at the UN and a legal
personality, will be handed what is left. That produces the Luttwak pattern in its sharpest form: the means that keep the Authority alive (coordination with Israel, endorsement of the
Trump plan, reform pledges to donors, a managed succession) are the same that drain its credibility with Palestinians, while the means that raise its standing abroad (157 recognitions, the
ICJ opinion, the ICC) are punished with the loss of money and travel. In 2025-26 the pressure came from three sides at once: Israel's fiscal strangulation and settlement drive (UN: 'the PA
is at the brink of collapse'), a US-designed Gaza order that includes technocrats but not the Authority, and Hamas, which is losing public support (24%) but not its arms. The Western wave of
recognition in September 2025 and the settlement-goods bans of 2026 are real, but they give the Authority diplomatic oxygen, not territory or revenue. Two signals that are not rows: Abbas telling
the UN on 24 Sep 2026 that elections were on and postponing them sixteen days later, and the US ban that again kept him out of New York. With Israeli elections on 27 Oct 2026, the PA's real
question is whether a new government in Jerusalem would unfreeze the clearance revenues or whether the money, not the flag, decides its survival.

grand_strategy.reading:
Qatar runs the strategy of a rich micro-state that has no army to match its
neighbours and therefore sells services in exchange for protection: gas to the
world, mediation to the great powers, money to the weak, and a base to
Washington. The strategy worked for thirty years because the bill was paid in
influence rather than force; since June 2025 the bill has come due. Israel
struck its capital with the United States on notice, Iran fired at it three
times and took out a sixth of its LNG capacity, and Hormuz showed that the whole
franchise exits through a single strait that the aggressor controls. The reply
is a reconstruction of deterrence: a written US guarantee (EO 14353, a
presidential order rather than a treaty), a Turkish tie, air defence that has
now shot down aircraft, and a vocabulary of Gulf self-sufficiency that Doha
shares with Abu Dhabi. Luttwak's pattern is the paradoxical one: each asset that
buys security (Al Udeid, Hamas as interlocutor, Iran as neighbour, LNG as
leverage) is the one that draws the fire. Two signals that are not rows: Qatar
refused in March 2026 to lead US-Iran mediation so that attacking it would not
earn Tehran better terms, and returned to the table by August; and Doha is
spending its mediation capital on the places where it still has leverage
(Gaza, DRC, Ukraine's children, Afghanistan) while the Iranian file belongs to
Pakistan. The next test is whether the written guarantee holds and whether
Hormuz reopens before buyers decide that Qatar is a risk to be hedged.

grand_strategy.reading: Romania is a frontline state with a rear-area politics. Its grand strategy is borrowed security: bind the United States, NATO and the EU to the Black Sea by hosting their bases, buying their arms with their loans and keeping Ukraine and Moldova alive as buffers. The method has worked in hardware (Kogalniceanu, Deveselu, F-35s, SAFE) and fails at the margin Washington controls: the brigade left in October 2025 while Bucharest was offering a base for the Iran operation five months later. What is new in 2026 is that the weak point is internal. The annulled election of 2024 did not remove the sovereigntist vote, a third of Parliament, and the fiscal repair that the EU and the rating agencies demanded took the coalition apart; the country has had a caretaker cabinet since 5 May and a fourth nominee since 5 October, with every agency one step above junk. Neighbours show the same split between kinship and interest: Moldova is kin and a partner, Ukraine is a partner and a dispute over Romanian schools, Hungary is a co-member whose new government (Magyar, April 2026) has restarted the conversation, Serbia is a partner it presses on the Vlachs, Turkey the one NATO ally in the Black Sea with ships and a strategic partnership. China is held at arm's length by law (the 5G rules that exclude Huawei) and, since Dan's remarks on the 2025 strategy, with open caution; Israel is a partner whose war Romania abstained on in 2023 and 2024 and voted for the Palestinian seat in 2026. Read through Luttwak, the danger is that Romania's policy of making itself useful rests on stable government in Bucharest, which is the thing it lacks.

grand_strategy.reading:
Russia in 2026 runs a grand strategy with one fixed aim - a Ukraine that is not a
state in the Western sense - and a shrinking set of means to reach it. At the
technical and tactical levels the war is being won slowly: Kursk retaken, 0.72% of
Ukraine gained in 2025, Oreshnik over Kyiv. At the level of theatre strategy it has
stalled: the front moves by villages, the price is a budget 40% military, a 21% key
rate and civilian investment in collapse, and the manpower comes from Pyongyang. At
the level of grand strategy the picture inverts, as Luttwak says it must: the move
meant to push NATO back brought Finland and Sweden in and Germany to rearm; the move
meant to free Russia from the West handed its trade, its currency and its machine
tools to China; the levers that hold Belarus pushed Armenia and Azerbaijan away. The
one genuine success since 2025 is diplomatic - the bilateral channel to Washington,
Riyadh to Anchorage to the 28-point plan - and it rests on a paradox too: the demand
for the Donbas is what keeps Trump talking and what keeps any talk from ending. Three
signals that are not rows: Ushakov quietly dropped the 'spirit of Anchorage' slogan
in mid-2026; the New Delhi BRICS declaration dropped Ukraine altogether; and Vucic
stayed away from the 2026 parade while Fico came and did not watch it. The culminating
point of this attrition war is visible from Moscow as from Kyiv; what Moscow has not
yet decided is whether the thaw with Washington is a way to stop before it or a way
to pass it.

grand_strategy.reading: Rwanda is Luttwak's small state that turns its vulnerability into a regional offensive and then sells security abroad to buy immunity at home. The vulnerability is real - a landlocked state of the 1994 survivors, with the perpetrators' successors (the FDLR) next door and a Congolese army that has used them - and Kigali has made it the license for a forward defence in the Kivus, run through the RDF and AFC/M23 (UN experts: command and control; Goma, Bukavu, Uvira). The surplus the offensive creates is spent twice: at home as rent (gold, tin, tantalum, mineral transit) that replaces falling aid, and abroad as a service (Cabo Delgado, the CAR, UN missions) that makes the West, Paris, Maputo and now Washington need the army it sanctions. The Washington Accords of 4 December 2025 were the best expression of that logic: peace for minerals, deportees and goodwill. But the accord has become a measuring rod, the US sanctioned the RDF on 2 March 2026 and on 13 October 2026 demanded unconditional withdrawal, the EU stopped paying for Mozambique, and the offensive has produced a second adversary in Burundi. Where Luttwak's paradox bites hardest is in the memory: the genocide is both the moral capital that buys immunity and the thing the offensive spends. The grade toward the DRC is rival, not adversary: Kigali's declared aim is security and leverage, not the end of the Congolese state, and it signed an accord with Tshisekedi; the FDLR is the real adversary, and AFC/M23 the instrument. Not verified for this card: the text of the Washington Accords (read through press), a 2026 UN experts' report, the number of RDF troops in 2026, the Benin deployment (the 2022 agreement is on record, a deployment is not), Rwandan policy toward Kenya and Tanzania in 2026, the Mozambique SOFA reported for August 2025, and any succession arrangement.

grand_strategy.reading:
Saudi Arabia is a rich state that has become a front-line state without
changing its aim, which is to buy time for an economy that will outlast oil.
Everything in the card is a trade of one scarce thing for another: US
protection against Israeli normalisation, a Pakistani and Turkish guarantee
against dependence on Washington, the UAE's exit from Yemen against a Houthi
front of its own, a wartime oil price against lost volume and market share.
The Luttwakian pattern is that each safeguard creates the next exposure: the
February 2026 war put Iranian missiles on Ras Tanura and Riyadh, the
answers (strikes in Iraq, an offensive in Yemen) brought the Houthis to the
capital's airport, and the hedges (Makkah pact, Pakistani troops) show a
kingdom unsure that the United States will fight for it. The thaw with Abu Dhabi
(July-October 2026) is tactical, since Yemen's south, Sudan and the Horn
remain contested. Signals that are not rows: the postponement, at Riyadh's
request, of the Hormuz talks between Gulf states and Iran in Sept 2026
(Saudi Arabia would rather the US negotiates than the Gulf legitimises
Iranian control of the strait); Egypt declining the Makkah pact while saying
Gulf security is its own; and the fiscal arithmetic that makes the 2026 deficit look
better only because the war lifts the price. Open gaps in this pass: the
OIC and Arab League as instruments, Afghanistan, Jordan, Kuwait, Oman, the
Horn beyond commentary, and an official Saudi source for the Houthi truce
breakdown (reports date the renewed fighting from June or July 2026).

grand_strategy.reading: Sudan is the Luttwak case of a state at war with its own instrument. The RSF was raised by the regime to guard it against its own army, and the generals who let it grow (Burhan took power together with Hemedti in October 2021) can neither win without destroying it nor accept a truce that leaves it standing. The Gulf and Egypt, which dealt with both generals before the war (the UAE promoted Hemedti's economic role), are now divided inside the Quad, so the army's strategy is a negotiation with its own sponsors: keep Cairo, Riyadh, Ankara and Doha, shut out Abu Dhabi, and avoid being sold a freeze of the lines by Washington. October 2026 finds it with momentum in Kordofan and on the wrong side of the US visa desk. Two signals that are not rows: the Russian naval base at Port Sudan, agreed in December 2020, has no source showing it ratified or built, so Moscow is a supplier and a reserve, not an anchor; and Burhan's postponed trip to the UN General Assembly in September, with his US visa reportedly withheld until he accepts a ceasefire, which shows that the state's own head is now a bargaining object for Washington. The paradoxes share one shape: each lever that wins ground (Islamist brigades, Iranian and Turkish drones, refusing the Quad) buys the army less standing with the people who will write the settlement.

grand_strategy.reading:
Singapore is Luttwak's small state that cannot win a contest of weight and so plays
the other game: it makes itself indispensable to everyone. It lodges the American navy
at Changi, buys American F-35s, trades more with China than with anyone, signs a
partnership with every capital that matters and keeps a budget near 3% of GDP for a
force that trains on other people's land. The logic is sound while the great powers
compete at a distance; it inverts when they collide, because the state that served
both is the first place where each can be denied to the other (the chip diversion
cases and the cyber intrusion are early tremors). Wong's doctrine for a disordered
world is to say so openly - rules for all, no forced choice, 'useful but not used' -
and to spend the political capital of a 65.57% mandate on shock absorbers: stored
wealth, replacement LNG, a 2061 water horizon and a Johor zone that turns the
neighbour from a lever into a stakeholder. What the strategy cannot fix is the
arithmetic underneath: a fertility rate of 0.87 and a labour force that must keep
arriving from abroad.

grand_strategy.reading: San Marino has no currency of its own and no independent trade policy, since the euro and the customs union bind it to Italian and EU rules. Its grand strategy is to keep the Italian and EU frameworks that guarantee its existence while turning its financial sector from a source of distinction into a regulated market. The Captains Regent speak for the state and the Secretariat carries the work. Its most important move, the Association Agreement, has been concluded but is not yet signed or ratified, so the reading of the 2026 steps stays provisional.
