NLD.note: A rival with a wound, not a mortal enemy in the ontology's sense: The Hague wants Russia's behaviour changed, sanctioned and judged, not its regime removed. The grievance is MH17: 196 Dutch nationals died on 17 Jul 2014; the ICAO Council (12 May 2025) and the European Court of Human Rights (9 Jul 2025, unanimous) held Russia responsible, and Moscow rejects both. The Hague summit declaration names Russia the main long-term threat, Rotterdam screens sanctioned ships and the government is writing laws against shadow-fleet tankers. If the RUS card grades the Netherlands 'adversary', the pair is asymmetric on purpose. Bond - grievance.

NLD.note: The key China episode is Nexperia: the Dutch state took control of the Chinese-owned chipmaker on 12 Oct 2025 (Goods Availability Act), Beijing banned the export of Nexperia China's chips from 4 Oct, European carmakers neared a stop, and The Hague suspended its order on 19 Nov 2025; litigation, a Chinese court freeze of about USD 300m (31 Aug 2026) and a split Nexperia continue. Since then the two have worked a 'pragmatic reset': Berendsen-Wang Yi call (13 Mar 2026, 'one of the most important bilateral relationships'), the first ministerial trade mission since 2018 (Sjoerdsma, July 2026). Meanwhile ASML's export controls (since 2023, under American pressure) cut China out of the most advanced machines. China is a trading partner worth about EUR 90bn a year (2024), so cooperation out of necessity while resisting alignment. No source calls it 'reluctant partner'; the grade is our reading (C). Bond - none.

NRU.note: Ally by treaty, not by defence. The December 2024 treaty gives Australia a say over Nauru's security, banking and telecommunications: no third-party engagement without Canberra's agreement. The ontology's own test for ally is a treaty, and the grade is Nauru's view of its own position, not Australia's. Australia's card reads the same treaty as partner ('not an alliance', no mutual defence); that is its reading of its side, and the two grades can differ. No source calls the relation reluctant, so reluctant ally is not used. Bond none: the tie is money and a veto, with no kinship, affinity or open grievance in the sources. Trend warming: the treaty was signed in December 2024 and the August 2025 memorandum extended it to the NZYQ cohort. Confidence B: one tier-2 and one tier-3 report of the treaty (ASPI, PINA), the treaty text not read; the 2025 memorandum rests on tier-3 press.

org-eu.note: Reluctant partner, not rival: the Union's own formula since the 12 Mar 2019 strategic outlook is partner, competitor and 'systemic rival', but the structure is a bloc that keeps trading with a power it distrusts, which is the definition of the grade. The instruments are those of a partner that resists: 'de-risking, not decoupling' (von der Leyen, 30 Mar 2023), countervailing duties of 7.8-35.3% on Chinese EVs since Oct 2024 (softened into minimum-price undertakings, first accepted 10 Feb 2026), export controls and investment screening; and on the other side the largest bilateral deficit the Union runs, a July 2025 Beijing summit that produced a climate statement, and on 8-9 Oct 2026 a ten-point trade list, fast-track rare-earth magnet licences and hybrid-vehicle terms. Not rival: the Union does not contain China and has no security dispute with it except through Russia; its largest members (Germany, the Netherlands) read Beijing as reluctant partner, and rival is the reading of those with a direct security stake (the United States, Japan, India, Australia, NATO). Not partner: Beijing's rare-earth licensing used as leverage (only just over half of about 2,000 priority EU applications processed by Oct 2025) and the Nexperia seizure and counter-seizure (Dutch order of 30 Sep 2025, Chinese court freeze of Nexperia BV's stakes on 31 Aug 2026) keep the resistance visible. Stable: managed on both sides. Bond none. Regraded from rival on 16 Oct 2026: the grade follows the structural position, not the communiqué.

org-eu.note: Rival, not adversary. org-nato.note: Rival, not adversary, in the ontology's terms. The 2022 Strategic Concept names Russia 'the most significant and direct threat' and the Ankara declaration (8 Jul 2026) 'the long-term threat', Eastern Sentry (12 Sep 2025), Baltic Sentry (Jan 2025) and two Article 4 sessions in September 2025 (Poland, Estonia) show the contest; NATO suspended practical cooperation in April 2014 and expelled eight Russian officials in October 2021, after which Moscow closed its mission. But NATO's declared aim is deterrence and defence, not the end of the Russian state or regime, and the channel for dialogue is kept formally open; Peskov himself said Moscow stays open to dialogue when there is a chance for constructive engagement. A threat label in an official text is the source for the hostile reading, the grade follows the structure (a standing deterrence contest, no allied war aim against Russia). Trend cooling: airspace violations (Estonia MiG-31s, 19 Sep 2025) and Russian drones in Poland rose in 2025-26. Bond - grievance: Moscow's reading of enlargement as encirclement, and NATO's of 2014 and 2022 as betrayal.

Structurally the United States is the guarantor and the founder (Article 5, the nuclear umbrella, about 80,000 troops in Europe, 57% of alliance spending), so this is an alliance and not a rivalry; the grade is reluctant_ally because the alignment is held by necessity under visible friction: the Pentagon's 'NATO 3.0' (Colby, Feb 2026), the cut to the Force Model (May-June 2026), 5,000 troops leaving Germany (announced 1 May 2026) and a posture review weighing 25,000-40,000 withdrawals, Trump's 'NATO WASN'T THERE WHEN WE NEEDED THEM' over the Iran war, doubts about Article 5 before Ankara and the Greenland coercion of Denmark (settled on paper on 22 Sep 2026). The duplication question (Albright's 'no duplication' of 1998) is the standing friction: SAFE loans are limited to EU states and exclude non-EU allies such as Turkey, the UK and Canada unless agreed. PHL.note: Rival, not adversary. The test is whether a declared aim is the other's defeat or disappearance, and neither side states one: Manila's aim is to keep what it holds and the award's zone, not to end the Chinese state, and it keeps the channel open while it protests (Lazaro met Wang Yi on 22 Jul 2026, the first foreign-minister bilateral in two years, raised the Ayungin baton incident and reaffirmed the One China policy in the same meeting). Beijing's aim at the shoals is control, removal of the Sierra Madre and, at Scarborough, a 'national nature reserve' (State Council, Sep 2025) - coercion short of war, not Manila's destruction. The friction is the sharpest in the region: Second Thomas Shoal baton assault (20 Jul 2026), water cannon at Scarborough on 23-24 Jul 2026, the Sabina ramming of 31 Aug 2024, a Chinese platform inside the Scarborough lagoon (May-June 2026). The pair is also tied by trade: China supplies 28.6% of Philippine imports. No source uses the word 'rival': the grade is our reading of the structure (confidence C), as for Kosovo toward Serbia. Trend stable: a first ministerial bilateral in two years, but incidents continue. Bond - grievance: the 2016 award that Beijing calls null, and the shoals taken in 2012.

PRK.note: Treaty ally under the 1961 Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance, whose 65th anniversary Xi invoked in Pyongyang on 8-9 Jun 2026; Kim called ties the 'top strategic priority'. The posture has gone cool and then warm: Pyongyang's turn to Moscow in 2022-24 thinned Chinese contact and trade fell 5% in 2024 (USD 2.1bn); Kim attended Beijing's parade on 3 Sep 2025 and met Xi on 4 Sep (their sixth meeting), trade rose 25% to USD 2.7bn in 2025, and Xi made his first visit in seven years. Analysts read Xi's trip as Beijing reasserting itself as 'the principal actor' in the North; the treaty and the 98% share of official trade are why this stays an alliance despite the resentment a dependent partner carries. Not graded reluctant_ally because the 2024 friction has been repaired in both leaders' public acts. Bond - affinity: party ties and the Korean War, not kinship.

PRK.note: Rival, not adversary - argued. For: Kim calls South Korea the 'most hostile' state and 'principal enemy', threatens to 'completely destroy' it if threatened, has cut roads and rails, fortified the line since 2024 and has made the doctrine constitutional. Against: the ontology reserves 'adversary' for a declared aim of the other's defeat or disappearance, and the doctrine of December 2023 says the opposite - Pyongyang gave up absorbing the South, wrote reunification out of the constitution (March 2026), defines the South as a bordering state and seeks separation, the destruction threat being conditional on attack. A state that fences itself off and denies the other state's claim to kinship is a rival with an arms race, not a mortal enemy; Seoul's own 'peaceful two-state' white paper (May 2026) treats it the same way. Cooling because the 2025-26 steps (Party Congress, border works, mines of 21 Sep 2026, rejection of every Seoul overture by Kim Yo Jong and the SPA speech) hardened the separation, not because of any thaw. Bond - kin: language, history and the 1948 founding claim; Pyongyang formally repudiates it, so the pair is a feud in Luttwak's sense and Pyongyang's repudiation is the bet, not yet the fact. The USA-PRK pair below is the real test of adversary and stays rival too.

What would make it adversary is the regime-change fear, and Kim cites it (US action in Venezuela, per analysts) as the reason the arsenal is permanent; but no document sets the American state's defeat as an aim. Warming from the Trump outreach (Trump on 19 Aug 2026: he will meet Kim 'later this year', Kim Yo Jong denies any contact); not warm enough to be a partner: the sanctions (OFAC designations of 12 Mar 2026), the ICBM and enrichment disclosures and the Bybit heist all point the other way. The hostility is real and one-sided in intent: the occupation (ICJ 2024: unlawful), the withholding of clearance revenues since May 2025, the E1 tenders of Aug 2026, the first Area A land seizure for settlements, settler violence at record levels (UN: about 1,430 incidents to 10 Aug 2026), and, per PISM, a coalition aim of blocking statehood and, if the far right wins, dismantling the PA. Israel's own grade of the PA may be harsher (build will flag the asymmetry if Jerusalem's card says adversary). No source uses the word 'rival': the grade is our reading of the structure (confidence C). Cooling: the Israeli election of 27 Oct 2026 is contested by blocs most of which oppose a Palestinian state (Al Jazeera). Bond - grievance: occupation, 1948 and 1967.

QAT.note: The grade rests on three official facts. Executive Order 14353 (29 Sep 2025) makes any armed attack on Qatar's territory, sovereignty or critical infrastructure a threat to the peace and security of the United States, with joint contingency planning and diplomatic, economic and, if necessary, military response; Qatar was designated a major non-NATO ally on 10 Mar 2022; and Al Udeid, the largest US base in the region (about 10,000 personnel), sits on its soil. Qatar buys the alliance with money: USD 243.5bn of announced deals during Trump's visit of May 2025 (arms of about USD 3bn), a Qatari Air Force facility at Mountain Home (Oct 2025), emergency-fast-tracked Patriot and APKWS replenishment (May 2026), a gifted 747 for Air Force One. It is `ally` rather than `reluctant_ally` because Doha chose and pays for the arrangement; the friction is real but does not change the structure: a US partner struck its capital on 9 Sep 2025 with Washington on notice, the order is an executive act, not a Senate treaty, and Qatar's spokesman now says the US alliance is 'important but insufficient' and that security self-sufficiency is 'the only way forward' while it deepens ties with Turkey and Pakistan. Bond none: interest, not kinship.

Ally and not partner: a stable de facto alignment on Somali soil against the same enemy, with the host government's consent and no alternative to it. No source uses the word 'rival': the grade is our reading of the structure (confidence C), and the neighbour cards differ (Poland grades Russia adversary, Czechia rival). Bond - grievance: the 2022 invasion that ended Swedish non-alignment, the airspace violations and the hybrid campaign.

SYR.note: Mirrors Turkey's own reading (TUR grades SYR ally). Ankara is the main backer of the post-Assad state: a military training agreement signed on 13 Aug 2025, reported talks on Turkish air bases (unconfirmed by either government), Turkish forces that the defence minister said have no immediate withdrawal plan, Azerbaijani gas delivered through Kilis, and the diplomacy that closed the SDF file. Graded ally on stable de facto alignment, not a treaty, and with no mutual-defence clause. Enab Baladi frames the agreement as 'constrained by limits' - Damascus keeps room to refuse bases - and the friction is external (Israel's strike on Abu al-Duhur, 18 Aug 2026). Bond - affinity: Sunni and Ottoman ties, not kinship.

SYR.note: The 10 Mar 2025 Abdi-al-Sharaa agreement, the Aleppo fighting of early January 2026 (at least 22 dead, tens of thousands displaced), the ceasefire and integration deal of about 18-30 Jan 2026 (government takes Raqqa, Deir ez-Zor, border crossings and the oil fields; SDF brigades enter the army in Hasakah and Kobani) and the SDF's own announcement on 25 Aug 2026 that it and the Autonomous Administration dissolved into the state. Damascus's aim is the end of an autonomous armed force, not a war of extermination, so `rival` (warming) and not `adversary`. Integration is self-reported and the number of 6,000 enlisted fighters comes from an unofficial government source; the Kurdish-language and decentralisation clauses remain untested. Bond - grievance: the 2025-26 fighting and a decade of YPG-Damascus separation.

TLS.note: Partner with a grievance. Australia's bugging of Dili's cabinet during the 2004 Timor Sea talks (the Witness K case, alleged) has not been apologised for: the charges against Bernard Collaery were dropped in July 2022, which Dili welcomed, but Canberra has not admitted the operation and no 2025 apology was found (HRLC, Jan 2024). The Albanese visit of 28-29 Jan 2026 produced a joint declaration, 'a new partnership for a new era': US$220m for human development, US$80m for private-sector development, US$8.2m for ASEAN and WTO participation, a 10% share of combined future upstream Greater Sunrise revenue to a Timor-Leste infrastructure fund (other reporting gives a larger share; not resolved here), and 10,000 Timorese workers in Australia by 2027-28. The friction is the field: Dili wants a pipeline to its south coast, Woodside prefers Darwin, and first gas has slipped to 2034-35. Grade partner rather than reluctant partner because the cooperation is broad and no source calls it grudging; trend stable because the declaration and the slipping gas talks pull in opposite directions.

TWN.note: Rival and not adversary, on purpose. Beijing claims the island, rehearses its blockade (Joint Sword 2024, Strait Thunder-2025A on 1-2 Apr 2025, Justice Mission-2025 on 29-31 Dec 2025, the closest live fire so far), punishes 'Taiwan independence diehards' (14 named plus 12 accomplices by 7 Jan 2026, rules of 21 Jun 2024 that allow the death penalty in absentia) and presses in the grey zone (cable cuts, coast guard). Taipei's own government calls China a 'foreign hostile force' (17 measures, 13 Mar 2025), which is the strongest source for the hostility, but its declared aim is to be left as it is and to talk 'on an equal and dignified footing' (Lai, 1 Jan 2026), not to end the Chinese state or its regime, so the mortal-enemy grade does not fit from Taipei's side; the ROC constitution's claim over the mainland is dormant, so claimed_territory does not apply either. The pair is asymmetric: Beijing's aim is the end of Taiwan's separateness. Trend stable: air activity in 2026 is half of 2025 while ships stay, Xi met KMT chair Cheng on 10 Apr 2026, and no named exercise has followed the Trump-Xi summits. No source uses the word 'rival'; the hostile reading itself rests on Taipei's own designation of China as a 'foreign hostile force' (13 Mar 2025), so confidence B (review, 2026-10-16): the atlas's placement is only between rival and adversary. Bond - kin: language, history and a shared civil war, which makes the pair a feud; Xi calls Taiwanese 'one family'.

TWN.note: Ally by structure, reluctant by friction. There is no treaty (the 1954 defence pact ended in 1979), but the Taiwan Relations Act, arms sales (a record USD 11.1bn notified in Dec 2025, USD 14bn approved by Congress in Jan 2026 and now held by Trump 'in abeyance'), training and the USD 250bn investment deal of Jan 2026 make the alignment stable and de facto; there is no alternative guarantor, which is why it is not a mere partner. The friction is visible and rising: Trump called the package 'a very good negotiating chip' after the Beijing summit (14-16 May 2026), said he is 'not looking to have somebody go independent', raised the Six Assurances question, hosted Xi on 23-25 Sep 2026 (Beijing says Xi asked the US to oppose independence; the White House fact sheet is silent on Taiwan), and Lutnick wants 40% of the chip chain moved to the US while the 15% tariff stays negotiable. Washington's own line is 'unchanged' (Rubio). Grade is our reading of structure (confidence C): sources describe the relationship as unofficial, strategic ambiguity and, since May, as transactional. Bond - affinity: democratic kinship, Congress and the Taiwanese diaspora; no grievance.

USA.note: The one 'adversary' of the card and the test case for the grade. For: Washington opened a war on 28 Feb 2026 whose stated reasons, in the President's own statement, included regime change; Trump had called for regime change on 17 Jan ('it's time'); the first strikes killed the Supreme Leader; a naval blockade was imposed on 13 Apr and reinstated on 13 Jul after a signed memorandum (17 Jun) collapsed; Tehran's new leader promises vengeance 'until fully achieved'. The NSS wants Gulf energy kept from 'an outright enemy' - its one use of the word. Against: Hegseth said it was not 'a so-called regime-change war', the June memorandum and the October demands (a 'meaningful' cut in enrichment, Hormuz reopened) are the terms of a settlement, and the State Department's legal note frames the operation as self-defence. The atlas reads it as a war between two states each of which would accept the other's defeat, with talks as an instrument of the war; if a settlement on enrichment and Hormuz holds, the grade becomes rival. Stable: the aim has not moved since February while the means have (blockade, strikes, memorandum, strikes again). Bond - grievance: 1979, the embassy, Beirut 1983, and now the base attacks (6,700 missiles and drones on US-hosting states by May 2026). Mirrors IRN's grade of the US (adversary, stable, grievance).

relations.summary: Kabul wants Pakistan to stop its air and drone strikes, reopen the border and transit trade, and accept that the Pakistani Taliban are Pakistan's internal problem; it says it is 'open to talks' and wants to discuss good neighbourliness, trade and security management. Islamabad's counter-demand is 'visible and verifiable' action against the TTP.

sources.title: Pakistan, Afghanistan hold talks in China to end months of conflict
Pakistan ready to reopen Afghan borders if Kabul tackles terrorism

relations.summary: The Emirate seeks the Afghan seat at the UN General Assembly; the Credentials Committee has deferred the claim every year since 2021 and Zelin reports a US 'silent hold'. The seat is still held by the credentials of the former republic's mission.

sources.title: Five Years of Taliban Diplomacy: Recognition Without Concessions
sources.publisher: Washington Institute for Near East Policy (Zelin)

sources.title: UN committee defers action on bid by Taliban, Myanmar junta to appoint envoys to world body

relations.summary: Muttaqi told the New York Times in mid-August 2026 that Washington could reopen its Kabul embassy and invest in minerals, dams and roads; the State Department refused in writing and said investment would enable repression. Washington's own demands (Bagram, prisoners, the women's bans, counter-terrorism) are unmet.

sources.title: Taliban foreign minister calls for reopening of US embassy in Kabul
US embassy in Kabul could reopen if Taliban changes policies, says former envoy
Washington distances itself from former envoy Khalilzad's Taliban meetings ahead of 9/11 anniversary

relations.summary: Kabul presses ahead with the Qosh Tepa canal (285 km planned; the first 108-km section commissioned) drawing on the Amu Darya, and its water minister says no agreement limits Afghan withdrawals. Tashkent signed a river-management framework with Balkh in May 2025 and seeks urgent water talks.

sources.title: Taliban commission first section of major canal that could threaten water sufficiency of Central Asia neighbours
Uzbekistan, Taliban sign agreement on water resources and economic cooperation
The Qosh Tepa canal: source of possible regional tension
sources.publisher: Institute of South Asian Studies, NUS

relations.summary: The Taliban seek to crush the National Resistance Front and its allied fronts, which in turn aim to end Taliban rule; the Emirate has lost one district centre briefly (Yaftali Sufla, July 2026) and the EUAA finds no armed group holding territory.

sources.title: Anti-Taliban resistance groups increase attacks in northeast Afghanistan, district centre briefly falls
Country guidance Afghanistan - resistance groups opposing the Taliban

relations.summary: Trilateral framework agreement among Uzbekistan, Afghanistan and Pakistan (Kabul, 17 Jul 2025) to prepare a feasibility study for the Trans-Afghan railway (Termez - Naibabad - Logar - Kharlachi, about 760 km, estimated USD 4.8-5bn). Uzbekistan ratified in February 2026; the Afghan and Pakistani steps are unconfirmed, and the Afghan-Pakistani war puts the Pakistani leg in doubt.

sources.title: Tashkent, Islamabad and Kabul sign agreement on feasibility study for Trans-Afghan railway
Uzbekistan ratifies feasibility study agreement for Trans-Afghan railway

relations.summary: The Emirate rejects the ICC outright; after the Pre-Trial Chamber issued warrants for the Emir Hibatullah Akhundzada and chief justice Abdul Hakim Haqqani (8 Jul 2025, gender persecution), Mujahid said the Taliban do not recognise any international court nor consider themselves bound by it.

sources.title: ICC issues arrest warrants for Taliban leaders
ICC issues arrest warrants for Taliban leaders over gender-based persecution in Afghanistan

relations.summary: Military-technical cooperation agreement signed 27 May 2026 by Defence Minister Mullah Yaqoob and Security Council Secretary Shoigu in Moscow. Kabulov called it a framework to repair and restore Soviet and Russian equipment; the text is unpublished and Yaqoob said it is not a defence pact. Not a security guarantee.

sources.title: Kremlin deepens Taliban partnership with new military-technical agreement
Taliban, Russia sign deal expanding military and technical cooperation

relations.summary: Taliban commerce figures of August 2026 put annual trade with Iran at USD 3.6bn, making Iran the largest trading partner; a Taliban spokesman reported USD 1.6bn with Iran in six months of 2025 against USD 1.1bn with Pakistan. About 1,300 trucks cross Islam Qala daily (March 2026). Figures are Taliban-reported (an Iranian consul in Herat said about USD 4bn); the World Bank release gives no share.

sources.title: Taliban: Iran is Afghanistan's largest trading partner
About 1,300 trucks cross daily as Afghanistan-Iran trade remains steady

relations.summary: The 2008 China Metallurgical Group (MCC) 30-year concession for Mes Aynak copper, worth about USD 3bn, restarted with a road and a groundbreaking in July 2024 after a 16-year delay; in 2025 the mine was reported nearing readiness and changed to underground mining, with production expected around 2026. Beijing also saw a 2023 contract for Amu Darya oil (about USD 540m) cancelled by the Taliban in 2025.

The Burkina state is not named as responsible; this row records the spillover, not a Burkinabe act.

Trade with Iran was about US$1.3m in 2025 (bne IntelliNews, opinion piece, tier 4).
relations.note: The statement is a government source (tier 1) cited in the Wikipedia foreign-relations article; the page itself was not fetched, so the date and wording are as cited. Peru had had an embassy in Tehran until 1978 and a lone ambassador from 1977.

issues.title: Taiwan
issues.subtitle: who recognises the Republic of China
issues.why: Twelve governments keep formal ties with Taipei; everyone else has chosen Beijing. The list shrinks every few years.

issues.title: Palestine
issues.subtitle: who recognises the State of Palestine
issues.why: The 2024-25 wave of Western recognitions moved the line that had stood since 1988.

issues.title: Kosovo
issues.subtitle: who recognises it
issues.why: Recognition is Serbia's and Kosovo's whole contest; five EU members still refuse, Belgrade campaigns for withdrawals.

issues.title: Ukraine
issues.subtitle: the last General Assembly vote on the war
issues.why: The February 2026 vote, with the United States abstaining, shows where the coalition stands four years in.

issues.title: Ukraine, March 2022
issues.subtitle: the first vote on the aggression
issues.why: The baseline - 141 in favour - against which every later vote on Ukraine is read.

issues.title: Annexations
issues.subtitle: the October 2022 vote on Russia's annexation of Ukrainian regions
issues.why: Territorial integrity is the one principle almost every state will vote for, even those close to Moscow.

issues.title: Srebrenica
issues.subtitle: the 2024 genocide remembrance vote
issues.why: Serbia campaigned against it and counted the 68 abstentions as a victory; the vote maps the Balkans' memory wars onto the world.

issues.title: Gaza
issues.subtitle: the 2024 vote to end Israel's presence in the territories
issues.why: The clearest line of the Gaza war in the Assembly, with the West split in three.

issues.title: Palestine at the UN
issues.subtitle: the September 2026 vote on Palestine's participation
issues.why: After the recognitions, the procedural vote that measures them.
